utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning. I apologise for the delay. We were due to begin at 10 o'clock. However, there have been some technical difficulties. We are still attempting to resolve the difficulties. I am told that the only remaining difficulty has to do with the video that is going out to the press. So, we will do what we can to resolve that. Oh, it is going out. OK, there are no technical difficulties! We have concluded the submissions of evidence and we will now hear from the parties regarding their positions, closing submissions. We have reserved today, tomorrow and, if necessary, Wednesday. The Prosecution will begin. We will then hear from the Defence and then, if requested, we will then hear from the Prosecution once again and the Defence by way of a rejoinder. Are you ready to proceed, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. May it please the Court, some 50 years ago the world recoiled in horror at the unspeakable carnage and destruction one group of human beings had inflicted on another. The reaction to that horror and destruction was the pledge "Never again". This Tribunal exists today, and you sit here today, because that pledge was not kept. Perhaps one of the witnesses to this trial best summarised why you are here today to decide this case. When asked about the colour of the police uniforms in Yugoslavia, witness S replied as follows: "The police of Yugoslavia, that is, the Yugoslav police had traditionally -- wore traditionally blue uniforms, but SDS took over the power and they had traditional powers and traditional uniforms and traditional authorities and traditionally wanted to kill us all. That is the tradition." You sit here today to break that tradition, a tradition whereby retribution for past grievances has been visited on present day members of the group held responsible for those perceived wrongs. Human beings do cry for justice for wrongs that are done upon them, but only through the rule of law can that justice ever be achieved. Only after an accused has been given a fair trial and the society whose laws were violated given a fair hearing can true justice be served. Much has been made of this trial and, indeed, the trial has required this Chamber to clarify, interpret and to implement, sometimes for the first time, the rules the Tribunal Chambers have adopted. There have been areas of international law that you have had to clarify and rule upon in this unique, international setting. But at the heart of all this, the role you are performing is the role that is performed at each and every criminal proceedings, to hear the evidence, to judge its credibility and, based on that assessment, to determine if the Prosecution has proven the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. That standard, the highest known to law, is the same in every criminal proceeding and is there for the same purpose, to ensure that an accused is convicted only if and only when the evidence is such as to exclude every reasonable doubt, that is, that an accused may only be convicted when the only reasonable explanation for the credible evidence is that the accused committed the offences. So too is the determination of credibility the same here as for any criminal trial. Based on your experience as jurists, your experience as human beings, you must critically evaluate the evidence given to you in the light of factors that are no different than the ones you would apply in your domestic jurisdictions. Much of the evidence you have received is in the form of witness testimony and, again, determining the credibility of witnesses is a task for fact finders in every criminal trial. The same factors you would apply in your jurisdictions apply here, considering the person's intelligence, their education, considering their ability to observe and accurately remember, considering what prejudices or biases they may have, what relationship, if any, the witnesses may have to either side, the extent to which the witness is supported or contradicted by other evidence and where there are possible contradictions, are those contradictions significant or minor? Are they the result of different ways of remembering, of the passage of time, or are they intentional untruths? In regard to claimed prior inconsistencies, an additional factor must be included in your deliberations here -- the problem of translation and interpretation. We have had countless examples of difficulties that exist when witnesses speak a language different than that spoken by investigators, attorneys and Judges. We are accustomed to putting great emphasis on the exact words of a witness. Remember here they are the exact words of an interpreter. It is not that the interpreters are unqualified -- they have performed superbly -- it is the inherent difficulty of interpreting a form of communication, human speech, that is so rich and subject to so many subtle differences. So, despite the many challenges this Trial Chamber has faced, the core of the task you have been performing and are now to perform is no different than any other criminal trial. If after careful evaluation of the evidence you determine that the Prosecution has not proven the elements of the offences beyond a reasonable doubt, you must acquit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I thought that the transcript went out for a moment, but it has not. OK.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, if after evaluating the evidence you determine that a reasonable doubt exists as to one or more elements of one or more offences, you must acquit of those offences. Conversely, if the Prosecution has proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt, your duty is to convict. The facts of this case will lead you to conclude you have a duty to convict. Before addressing the proof of the offences charged, it might be helpful to take a very brief look at the context in which these offences were committed. Former Yugoslavia was an area controlled by various empires throughout history, including a medieval Serbian empire. The history and political movements of the region fostered nationalistic sentiments in some areas, including Serbia. Demographic patterns and various historical factors created within the Serb national group a wish for a greater Serbia, one entity where the Serbs would be all together. The nationalistic views and goals of some areas of the former Yugoslavia, including the goal of a greater Serbia, waxed and waned throughout the last 130 years or so, as different groups were in power or in privileged positions within the area and as wars affected the region. Bosnia Herzegovina was historically, and up until 1992, a very diverse area, with the three main ethnic groups intermixed to a great degree. There was no one group that had a clear majority to superimpose its will on the others. Marshal Tito, through the force of his personality as much as through his actions, managed to forge the former Yugoslavia into a Federal Republic with Belgrade as its centre. When he died, the unity he had forged soon followed. Nationalism was again on the rise, fanned inside Serbia, and to a significant degree outside Serbia as well, by the militant nationalistic propaganda of Slobodan Milosevic. Not only did he appeal to the nationalism of Serbs inside and outside Serbia, but he also became a catalyst for the other Republics, such as Slovenia, to respond in kind, based at least in part out of a fear of a Serbian rule in the region. The new constitutions of the Republics more homogeneous than Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia, reflected the nationalistic aim of a preferred status for their own ethnic group. You have heard testimony about the preamble to the constitutions of Slovenia, Croatia and Serbia, all of those by the language indicating a desire that the predominant ethnic group would be in a favoured position in these new states. For whatever reason, a practical reason because there was no clear majority, or because of a more philosophical reason, a true wish to embody the goals of a unified country of equals, the Bosnian Constitutional preamble does not include this nationalistic language, but rather refers to "We peoples, mentioning Muslims, Serbs and Croats". Although, eventually, Serbia itself became part of the new independent entity of the FRY, the Federal Republic of Serbia, when the movement towards independence began in Slovenia and Croatia, it was opposed by Serbia, Serbian elements in the federal leadership and by the JNA. At some point, the JNA ceased to exist and to function as the army of the peoples of Yugoslavia and, effectively, became the army of the Serbs whose task was to ensure that the vast majority of Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina would be part of and protected by the same Serbian-controlled state to which Serbia itself belonged. This led to JNA fighting in Croatia, not in order to restore a heterogeneous, unified Yugoslavia, but rather to achieve the goal of a Greater Serbia, a common area and state where all Serbs would be united.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Miss Hollis, what effect would you give to the testimony of Dr. Hayden, Professor Hayden, who was called by the Defence? If I recall his testimony correctly, it seems to me that he gave us a different picture and that is instead of Greater Serbia motivations being the catalysts for Slovenia and Croatia, it seems to me that his testimony related more to their own desires for independence, Slovenia and Croatia, and that thereafter there was no alternative left to the Bosnian Serbs within Bosnia-Herzegovina other than to take the action that they did. In fact, as I recall his testimony, he said that war was inevitable. The reason I recall that is that I recall my asking him a question about it because I was just hoping that, perhaps, war is not inevitable, but that relates more to the reaction on the part of the Bosnian Serbs. But it seems to me that his testimony, to the extent that it is even necessary for this Chamber to make a determination as to what was the cause of the conflict, was presented in a different way in terms of responsibility. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. First of all, your Honour, certainly I do believe that the evidence shows that when Tito died various areas, as I mentioned, especially the areas that were more homogenous in their population, began to think of themselves as an independent entity and began to move towards that. I think Dr. Hayden talked about that. I think though, however, on cross-examination he did admit that, in fact, in an article he had written earlier he had indicated that one of the factors in pushing these countries toward independence, in particular Slovenia, was the very, very strident propaganda, nationalist propaganda, that began to come out of Serbia when Milosevic took over. So that one of the factors in the nationalistic stance that Slovenia took, and certainly not the only factor, but one of those factors, was in response to their fear of this very militant Serbian propaganda and their fear that, in fact, Serbia was attempting to become the primary dominant figure in the region. As to the reaction of the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia, I believe again he admitted that he had written articles talking about the very, very aggressive fighting and dominance by the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia and that it was supported by the JNA. It was supported by Serbia. The reason that they could be so aggressive and they could demand war instead of trying to reconcile differences was because they had the backing of the JNA and the backing of Serbia. So, given the context that we suggest existed at the time, that is, the reemergence, for whatever reason, on the part of Serbian peoples of this desire to be united into one entity, that, yes, war was inevitable, because unless they could through the vote, not just the referendum keeping Bosnia with Serbia, but also at the local levels and the Republic levels, unless they could win a clear majority to ensure that Bosnia would do as Serbia wished, then the only way they could achieve that was through the force of arms. That eventually is what happened. Because of the mix in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were not able to achieve a clear majority. The governments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you will recall, were basically mixed after the elections because of the ethnic compositions of the areas. So not able to forge a clear majority through the polling places, they forged their own dominance by the use of force. It was the JNA turning its role from being the army of the peoples of Yugoslavia to being the vehicle of the Serbian wish for a united Serbian people that enabled them to move to violence and not really to have to seriously consider reconciliation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then the Bosnian Serbs, of course, were the minority. As I recall there was testimony that the Bosnian Serbs had boycotted the elections so that, given the fact they were a minority coupled with the fact of boycotting the election, there was little chance, I suppose, for the election to come out in favour of the greater Serbia notion, I guess. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would suggest, yes, your Honour, it certainly meant, by the boycott meant, that they would not be able to voice their desire to stay in Bosnia. From, apparently, almost 97 or 98 per cent of the people who did vote voted for independence. If that was a mix of Croatian peoples as well as Muslim peoples, then even had the Serbs voted, they may very likely have not been able to establish enough of a vote to defeat the referendum. We have had some evidence here that not all the Serbs did boycott the referendum, many of them did but some Serbs did vote in that referendum. There is evidence that some Serbs voted for independence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is in the context I have just spoken of that we turn to proof of the common elements of Articles 2 and 5. For Article 2, of course, we have to prove the existence of an international armed conflict and the protected status of the victims. For Article 5, we have to prove that there was a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population. Turning first to the requirement that the Prosecution prove the existence of international armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when you evaluate the evidence you will see that we have done so. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the conflict in Bosnia continued to be international after 19th May 1992, and that the victims of the crimes committed by the accused were protected persons within the meaning of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. As to the classification of the conflict, the Appeals Chamber in its decision on the Defence motion regarding jurisdiction, held that the conflict in the former Yugoslavia had been rendered international at least until 19 May 1992. It went on to indicate that, to classify the conflict as international after that date, direct involvement of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia must be proven. In fact, the evidence we have presented to you does prove that continuing direct involvement by the FRY. That evidence ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you go on, I will ask the Defence this question, but, do you understand the evidence of the Defence to challenge the existence of an international conflict, or do you consider that their evidence really related to once again Professor Hayden's testimony? I am not sure that really went to whether or not there existed an international conflict or whether the conflict was international or instead who was responsible, who was the catalyst. Do you view the Defence as challenging the existence of internationality in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that one portion of Dr. Hayden's testimony may have that impact, and that is the portion where he talks about whether the action in holding a referendum and then declaring independence was, in fact, a constitutional action on the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I suggest that it maybe an interesting academic argument, but the reality is that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the international community as independent. Therefore, the independence of that country is a proven fact. I believe that is the extent to which the evidence would challenge the internationality of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But that is just one leg, I suppose, of your argument that this was an international conflict, that is, the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- as a separate state and it is admittance into the United Nations. The bulk of your argument really relates to the involvement of the JNA and the reconstituting of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour, because I believe that is really the fundamental issue that must be addressed. Even though perhaps not challenged by the Defence, it would, of course, have been a finding you would make in order to find the accused guilty of the Article 2 offences. Your Honour, we have highlighted for you some of the evidence that proves the continuing involvement of the FRY after 19th May 1992. As we indicated in what may be considered a disclaimer in the written submissions we made, we have attempted to provide you with extracts of evidence and with certain points of evidence we believe are significant, but we do not in any way claim that to be an exhaustive listing. We are certain that there is additional evidence you will find as you do your own evaluation of the evidence in this case. But some of the evidence that would point and prove beyond a reasonable doubt the continuing participation of the FRY in this conflict after 19th May would be the following: The evidence of the use of JNA helicopters to fly the Muslim prisoners from the JNA barracks in Bijeljina, Bosnia, to the JNA base at Batajnica in Serbia on approximately 4 May ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can interrupt you for a moment? Can you explain to me how much you will be repeating what we already have in your quite detailed proof of international armed conflict and how much is new?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To some extent, your Honour, it will be repetition of those factors. If your Honours are satisfied with that and do not wish that repetition ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, no, I am not stopping you. I am just wanting to know how much I should note.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Most of it, your Honour, is indeed contained in the written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As I indicated, when Muslims prisoners were taken on approximately 4th May from Bosnia to Serbia, they were taken there in JNA helicopters. They were taken from the JNA barracks in Bosnia to a JNA air base in Serbia. Prisoners were kept at the air base and were later transferred to other JNA prisons in Serbia until they were exchanged to Croatia in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you again, but if you are going to give us new material, it is going to be enormously lengthy for us to trace it down to the 6,000 pages of transcript. If you can usefully give the transcript reference, that would help very much.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and when it is something new I will tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. While these prisoners were in JNA prisons in Serbia, the Muslims and Croats were subjected to the same types of beatings and torture by the JNA guards as they were in these JNA installations in Bosnia. Additional evidence of the continuing involvement of the FRY includes the UN Security Council resolution, Prosecution Exhibit 60, in which the Security Council imposed sanctions on the FRY in part for its failure to meet the conditions to remove JNA forces from the territory of Bosnia or place them under the jurisdiction of the Bosnian government. It also includes the evidence of the direct support of paramilitary units from Serbia by the JNA and the police. It includes the presence of the Podgorica Corps of what was then the VJ, the army of the FRY, conducting military operations in Bosnia through the summer and fall of 1992. As noted in the written submissions, Mr. Doko indicated that in his testimony. It also includes reports of artillery attacks from Serbia on to positions in Bosnia. Both Colonel Kranjc and Mr. Vulliamy testified concerning that. It includes the evidence of military and paramilitary units and equipment crossing into Bosnia from the Republic of Serbia in August 1992 in the area of Loznica, Serbia, and Mr. Vulliamy talked to you about that and that was part of the discussion of his visit there before going to Omarska camp. You will recall at that time as well that he spoke with prisoners held at that camp in Serbia and they could look across the river to their homes in Bosnia. We suggest that such evidence of the continuous military action by the FRY and its army in support of the conflict in Bosnia is sufficient of itself to prove that the conflict in Bosnia continued to be international beyond 19th May 1992. However, in addition to this direct involvement, the facts also provide a second basis for the determination that this armed conflict was international in character. The evidence confirms that after 19th May 1992, the relationship between the Republika Srpska, the Serbs in Bosnia and the supposed new army, the VRS, the army of the Serbs in Bosnia, the relationship between them and the FRY was certainly one of dependence -- the Bosnian Serbs being very dependent upon the FRY and upon the FRY military -- but it went beyond mere dependence. In fact, both politically and militarily, the Republika Srpska and the VRS acted as an organ of the FRY and in concert with the FRY for the attainment of a common goal. That stated goal was to maintain the territories claimed as part of Republika Srpska as part of this "greater Serbia". The conflict which began in Bosnia at the end of 1991 involving Serbian forces was conceived, planned and initiated by the Serbian authorities in Belgrade led by Slobodan Milosevic, and was accepted and implemented without reservation by the SDS leaders in Bosnia and Croatia. As determined by the Appeals Chamber and proven by the evidence in this case, the JNA was directly involved, along with local Territorial Defence units, police forces and paramilitary forces in all phases of the conflict in Bosnia prior to May 19th. The same political and military authorities continued to direct and control the conflict in Bosnia after May 19th and up to the conclusion of hostilities. If you would look ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you, how or what conceivable weight do we give to what the Appeals Chamber says as to matters of fact when it heard no evidence?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that you have to independently determine matters of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. So that when you say, I think you refer to the Appeal Chamber and its finding as to internationality, that is something we have to accept its views on international law, but not on the facts?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you will recall -- if you will look at the diagram that we are putting on the Elmo -- in regard to the fact that very little changed at the officer levels after 19th May, you will recall the testimony of retired Colonel Selak who prepared many charts for you, only one of which I will use, and that is the chart where he was basically showing you what the composition of the senior Officer Corps of the Fifth Corps was after this supposed creation of a new army, after 19th May. As you recall, many of the people -- in fact, most of the senior leaders -- were in the same position. There was one change, and that was at a lower level where a non-Serb was, in fact, replaced by a Serb. As you will recall that chart, you will recall that the double red Xs on that chart indicate to you that these are officers who are Serbs from Serbia who continued to serve in their positions after this supposed split of the two armies. We suggest to you that the evidence proves that the creation of the VRS and the VJ on 19th May 1992 was nothing more than an act of political expediency. Why was it felt necessary to do this? It was felt necessary to do this because of the response of the international community and the fear of Serbia, that the international community would respond if they did not do something to make it appear that they had withdrawn from this conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, in fact, what they did is what they did in many instances, and that is they told the world community what the world community wanted to hear and then they continued to do what they wanted to do. That is what happened in this instance. In that regard, your Honour, you, Judge McDonald, have asked on a couple of instances questions that perhaps have a component of who started the war, why was the war started, and at one point you asked even if you had to determine that. We suggest that you do not have to determine why it was started in the sense of, was it a war of aggression? We have not charged a war of aggression. The comments that I am making in argument in no way suggest that this was a war of aggression. It is not an element that has to be proven. It was not charged. The Serbs, for whatever reason, did what they did. It could have been because of their history and their fear of renewed outrages against them. For whatever reason, what they did made this an international conflict, made it a widespread or systematic attack and made it persecution. So, to the extent my remarks may appear to be arguing that this was a war of aggression, they are not intended that way, nor do we believe it is an issue that must be resolved by this Chamber. Again we believe that there is a great deal of evidence to prove that this dependent relationship, this consort of action, between the FRY and the Republika Srpska continued after 19th May 1992. Some of the examples of that are examples that have been given to you and that has to do with what really happened when the VRS and the VJ, that is, the army of Republika Srpska and the army of the FRY, split. The answer to that is very little different happened. Units were redesignated and became units of the VRS, but every one of those had been a unit of the JNA. As I mentioned, the commanding staff of those units remained virtually the same. The Commander of VRS and the Generals of the main staff of the VRS had all been Generals in the JNA. Many were appointed to their positions by the General Staff of the JNA at the time of the redesignation. Main staff maintained direct communication links with the General Staff of the VJ. You recall Colonel Selak telling you that in order to contact General Mladic he went through a Belgrade number. So it really was business as usual in all significant respects after this supposed breakup of the JNA into two armies. The role of the JNA units across Bosnia in assisting the SDS to take over power in the various municipalities and the subsequent attacks prior to May 19th were conducted by the same officers who continued to work hand-in-hand with the same political leaders to conduct the conflict after 19th May. The direction from the JNA General Staff for the removal of all soldiers from Bosnia -- again this was primarily related to conscripts, not to officers but to the lower ranking enlisted Corps -- who were citizens of the FRY and to remove or to return to Bosnia all conscripts who were from Bosnia, we suggest that that order, that direction, was motivated more out of a concern about how well conscripts from different Republics might fight for Bosnia and for the Serbs than from any intention to withdraw the FRY army from Bosnian soil. This reasoning and this action was in line with the principle followed by the JNA throughout the conflicts in Croatia and in Bosnia, that is, to rely on local Serb forces and paramilitary extremists as the front line infantry troops for attacks in the various regions, and to bolster the army cadre of conscript soldiers. The JNA's main contribution in this area was focused on the use of its heavy weapons, the heavy artillery, the rockets, the tanks, on the use of air power, on the logistics and the commanding control components. All of the officers of the JNA who remained in Bosnia after 19th May 1992 continued to be paid from Belgrade by this supposedly new army, the army of the FRY, the VJ army. In addition, personnel matters such as retirement requests were addressed and approved in Belgrade, not in Bosnia. Personnel records of the officers continued to be maintained in Belgrade, not in Bosnia. The JNA and then the VRS provided direct support to paramilitary units from the Republic of Serbia for their attacks and other operations in Bosnia. When the JNA or the VJ operating in Bosnia used the paramilitary units for their operations, the units then came under the operational control of the VJ even while they were operating in Bosnia. The JNA assisted in organising and training paramilitary forces and local Serb military and police forces in Bosnia, and these forces then took part in the attack there. It also organised, equipped and armed Serb Territorial Defence units in Bosnia. These units were all led by regular JNA officers who continued to lead them after this supposed split. Of course, the VRS continued to receive all of its logistical support from Serbia, and in regard to how it got that support, what the procedures were, who was called, there was really no difference. It was again business as usual. The evidence that you have in the record before you suggests no other reasonable explanation but that Republika Srpska and the VRS were acting as organs of, or in concert with, Serbia with FRY and with the VJ in the actions that took place after this supposed split. This argument, of course, involves a balance on your part, a very important balance, and that is, it is a balance, on the one hand, of the right of nations to determine their own foreign policy and to engage in foreign relations with other states. The balance, on the other hand, however, is the right of a country to be free of such involvement from the outside in a conflict in its country, that, in effect, the outside country has become a participant in the hostilities. So, I believe that is the balance you have to make. There is a point at which, even though states have wide latitude in determining their foreign policy and their foreign affairs, their involvement in conflict in another State is of such significance, is such an integral part of that conflict in the other state, that the international community must step in and say, despite disclaimers from that country, that the country has become involved to such an extent it is a participant and the conflict has become international. That, I believe, is the balance that has to be looked at and has to be struck based upon the facts that are provided in each case. We suggest here that balance falls on the side of such intensive, such extensive, such integral connection between what was happening in Bosnia and what FRY was doing, both with its troops in Bosnia, with its support of Bosnian Serbs, that it was so integrated into that conflict that the balance become struck in favour of saying it was an international conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know that I fully understand that. The balance of the right of states to engage in foreign relations with the right of a country to be free from involvement from an outside, from another ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- country in a conflict within their own country? Are you saying that it is the right of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to engage in foreign relations or are you focusing on the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Every state has that right and, of course, the FRY had that right to be involved in foreign relations. There are some types of support for hostilities in other countries that would not rise to the level of making it international. The Nicaragua case that has been discussed before you indicates that, indeed, you can have involvement through foreign relations providing support, providing assistance, providing perhaps some type of training, and that support would be basically for a country, a state, engaging in its right to be involved in relations with other countries, with other groups, and to determine a foreign policy. So there are some levels of involvement pertaining to a conflict elsewhere which would not make it international in scope. However, there is a point at which that involvement is so great that, indeed, it can be said that the country, the outside country, providing for that support or that direct involvement has become a participant. It is certainly not, we suggest, for this Tribunal or perhaps for any International Tribunal to say that a country may not take actions in support of groups that are in conflict in other countries. That would be an absolute ruling that, perhaps, would unduly infringe upon the right of states to be involved in foreign affairs and to pursue their own foreign policy goals. But what we are saying is there comes a point at which that involvement is so significant that the international community has a right to say, through a Tribunal such as this or other body, that that country has, in fact, become embroiled, enmeshed, in the conflict itself and that transforms the conflict into an international conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We, unlike Nicaragua, this Tribunal is not seeking to ascribe any state responsibility; instead what we are doing is to determine individual responsibility. So, to that extent even, the standard enunciated in Nicaragua may be a very different standard.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not an exact fit.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. The common element of Article 2 also includes the requirement that we prove that the status of the victims in this indictment were protected persons under the 1949 Geneva Conventions. Again, once you review the evidence that has been presented to you, you will conclude that that evidence proves this common element beyond a reasonable doubt. There is no question that Dragan Lukac, Fadil Redzic and Sulejman Tihic were protected persons within the meaning of the Geneva Conventions when they were seized by members of the JNA or those acting on its behalf prior to May 19th 1992. Similarly, there can be no doubt that the victims named in the indictment and the thousands of other unnamed Muslims and Croats represented in count 1 were seized, detained, maltreated and persecuted by the accused and other Serbs in opstina Prijedor were protected persons within the meaning of the Conventions. Article 4 of the Geneva Convention IV, Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War, states: "Persons protected by the convention are those who at any given moment and in any manner whatsoever find themselves in the case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a Party to the conflict or Occupying Power of which they are not nationals". The evidence provided to the Trial Chamber in the motion phase of the proceedings and, in particular, in Prosecution Exhibits 61, 63, 74 and 76 have established that the FRY and BiH were required to abide by the obligations of Geneva Conventions. The evidence in this case clearly establishes that the accused and the other Serb forces, including the military, the police and irregular forces were operating as an organ of, or on behalf of, or in concert with the FRY. In such an instance, the Bosnian Muslim and Croat victims who are the subject of this indictment may be regarded as having been "in the hands" of the FRY at the time they were being subjected to the conduct alleged in the indictment. On 23rd May 1992, the forces that attacked Kozarac were led by and under the control of military units staffed and commanded by soldiers and officers who only four days prior had been designated as the JNA. Those Commanders were implementing the strategy and tactics that had been devised by the JNA General Staff and Serbian political leaders. They were simply continuing the same type of operation to achieve the same goal as had been conducted in the other areas of eastern Bosnia prior to 19th May, that is, to destroy and remove the physical impediments to a greater Serbia. That activity continued in the months and years after May 19th 1992 in the exact same fashion and through the same military and political leaders as had been conducted prior to 19th May. The victims of the crimes committed in opstina Prijedor between May and December 1992 clearly fall within the wide protection of the Conventions. As indicated in the commentary to Article 4, that Article was drafted with the intent to provide the widest possible protection. The phrase "at any given moment and in any manner whatsoever" was intended to ensure that all possible situations were covered. The phrase "in the hands of" similarly "must be used in an extremely general sense ... [it] need not necessarily be understood in the physical sense. It simply means that the person is in the territory which is under the control of the power in question". That comes from a commentary to Article 4. Even if we accept that the announced division of the JNA into the VJ, that is, the army of the FRY, and the VRS, that is the army of Republika Srpska, did in fact create two armies, there is no doubt that the Serb forces in Bosnia after 19th May were acting on behalf of the FRY and in concert with the FRY and that, therefore, the Muslim and Croat persons in the opstina Prijedor can be treated as being in the hands of the FRY and, as a consequence, were protected persons under the Geneva Conventions. There is no evidence to suggest that any of the victims in the counts which charge violations of Article 2 were combatants and, therefore, not within the provisions of Geneva Convention IV. Even if the Trial Chamber were to consider the issue as being in question, it would not affect the validity of the charges, nor would it deprive the victims of their protected status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I could interrupt you to ask you where does this really get you? We are not, of course, trying the JNA, nor the FRY. You say it is clear that they find themselves in the hands of the FRY, in effect, which must be interpreted very widely. How does that bear on the accused? How is the accused to be distinguished from, say, some Serb or Croat or Muslim who happens to mistreat for his own pleasure and satisfaction somebody that he comes across who happens to be a protected person?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As to why we are focusing on the JNA, your Honour, is to satisfy the common element of Article 2, that is, to show an international conflict and, secondly ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- that they were protected. As to a person who just for his own purposes would mistreat a Croat or a Muslim, if that person was mistreating them for their own purposes and also with knowledge that that mistreatment was part of a widespread or systematic attack, that would then also, if a widespread or systematic attack existed, make that a crime against humanity. In other words, a person may be acting for more than one purpose. If the only reason they are acting is out of a wish of their own to harm someone, and they are not aware that this was part of and would advance a widespread or systematic attack, it would not fall under the Article 5 crimes. In regard to Article 2, we would suggest that if there is an international conflict, if the victim is a protected person and if the perpetrator is someone who is acting within the military or the police or the paramilitary units who are carrying out this conflict against these protected persons, then it would still transform that into a violation of Article 2. Again, if it is a person who simply on their own, is in the opstina, takes this as an opportunity to enact revenge, perhaps, against someone, then we would say, no, that would not transform that crime into a violation of Article 2 or into a violation of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Or, indeed, that crime, if one can call it a crime, would not be within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, it would not, your Honour. We need more than that. We need the person to be committing these crimes, it may be for personal motives as well, but permitting or committing these crimes in some capacity that is linked with the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is your basis for saying that there is no evidence that any of the victims were combatants? What is the meaning of a "combatant"? In the traditional sense, I suppose, in traditional wars, then if we go back to World War II, perhaps, except for the resistance, people wore uniforms. Someone had a different uniform from someone else. You could easily tell that somebody was a combatant. Here, though, we have heard testimony that sometimes there were not common uniforms, that soldiers wore different uniforms because there may have been a shortage of uniforms. We have heard testimony that sometimes individuals would try to defend their homes. In Jaskici, for example, and Sivci there was an attempt, if I recall the testimony, to defend; does that make the defender a combatant?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Traditionally, your Honour -- the reason that I mention combatant in this context is to show another potential category of protected persons -- a combatant would be seen as one who was part of an organised armed force, who was a member of that organised, recognised military, who wore a uniform, who was in a formal chain of command, who bore arms openly and also who was a person who was subject to the requirements of the Geneva Conventions. That is the clearest example of a combatant. In the law of war, as it has evolved, we have looked at other persons who could be also considered combatants. That would be persons who were part of a formal paramilitary unit where they also had a distinctive uniform for that unit, they had a very formal chain of command for that unit, they bore arms openly, they also were responsible to follow the requirements of the Geneva Conventions. Those also would be combatants. Another example of people who could transform themselves into some type of combatant would be when an area is attacked by a force, and the civilians in that area rise up to protect their homes. Then perhaps they could be considered a levy en masse and they would be also given combatant status. The significance for us here is that there has been some evidence of some loosely united groups in Kozarac, civilian groups, who performed sentry duty in the town, almost what you might call neighbourhood protection, neighbourhood watch groups. There were also some people in the TO there, and the TO had been mobilized the prior year, Territorial Defence, had been lawfully mobilized the prior year. There were a few of those people in the Kozarac area who performed functions of, perhaps, security and, sort of, overlooking what was going on. They were in the Kozarac area as well. How would they fit into this concept of combatant? We suggest that in the facts given you, they do not fit into that because they, sort of, got together on their own, they were very loosely organised, if at all. If any chain of command existed, it was a very, very loose one. It was not an effective one, so it did not meet the requirements for them to become a combatant force. If you were to look at that and determine that this, perhaps, 100 people or so in Kozarac had at some point become an entity you could characterise as a combatant force, then once they are captured, their status is still protected because it is no longer protected as a civilian, however now it is protected as a prisoner of war. That is the significance of what status a person might have. The evidence that you have in this case shows that the crimes that had been charged here occurred after the victims were within the custody and control of the accused and other Serb forces. At that time, even if there was an issue about what their status was previously, they were protected. They were protected as civilians, which is what we suggest they all were, or they were protected as combatants, as prisoners of war, people who had been taken out of combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You just said "in the hands of the accused and other Serb forces".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The whole of the evidence suggests that this accused was intent on avoiding the status of being a member of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would disagree with that interpretation, most respectfully. What I would suggest is the evidence shows that prior to being told he had to go to the front lines and fight, this accused was very willing to carry out the objectives of the conflict, of the attacks, in opstina Prijedor. What we believe the evidence suggested and proves to you is that this accused did become part of this force on 4th May, as the certificate shows; that he was involved in various capacities throughout this time but as a part of this force; that in fact on 4th May he was mobilized, he was given his orders, and on 4th May (and from that time on) he had a very clear part in what was to happen. So that, indeed, at some point he tries to avoid the frontlines, but he did not try to avoid carrying out what happened in opstina Prijedor, what happened in Kozarac. He was willing to remain there, to remain there and to ensure that the Muslims were gone from there, but he was not willing to go to the front lines and fight. That is the point at which he was no longer willing to go along with this. That is what we believe the evidence proves.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you have to be a member of the JNA -- you are speaking of internationality now. Your argument is that the JNA was present before May, 18th/19th, 1992 and that that makes it an international conflict. After May 18th or 19th of 1992, then basically the official forces of the Republika Srpska were acting in concert with and as agents of the forces of Serbia, and that Serbia, therefore, was so related to the armed forces, the official armed forces, if I may call it, that the forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina were acting as agents or were in concert with Serbia. Therefore, it not only makes it an international conflict, but it makes persons who are victimized at the hands of an aggressor a protected person. But the aggressor need not be a member of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do have to make the showing of an intent and you have to make the showing of a nexus, because offences happen during conflicts and sometimes they are totally individual, in that people are going on their own mark to get back at a neighbour because the neighbour knocked down his fence or whatever and has nothing to do with furthering the conflict. But if you can show that the acts were taken in furtherance of the conflict, then the aggressor need not be a member of official armed forces, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. There has to be the nexus.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have to show the nexus.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The nexus between your actions or the actions of the perpetrator and the ongoing armed conflict. There has to be that nexus. It does not have to be a member of the military, a member of the police, indeed not even a member of paramilitary, as long as the actions have a nexus with the conflict, with what is trying to be achieved by the side with whom the nexus is established. In regard to the argument about why this continued to be an international conflict, yes, one of our arguments is that the FRY continued to have such an involvement that basically the Bosnian Serbs were acting as agents or in concert with. We also suggest that the evidence proves that, in addition to that, FRY continued to be directly involved because they sent their own units into Bosnia and continued to do so after 19th May in Bosnia. So that there was direct involvement and there was also this, if you will, secondary involvement. Certainly we are not suggesting that the accused was part of the armed forces, although at some point, perhaps, he could have been; nor do we believe it is necessary that he be part of the armed forces, but again he must be someone who has a nexus with the conflict, for purposes of Article 2. He must be someone, for purposes of Article 5, who knows that his acts are something that will contribute to the widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. We do believe that the accused was acting either in a capacity, in military or with the police, in the actions that were carried out here or later, of course, as one of the political people in the opstina, one of the SDS political people in the opstina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will speak to the meaning of nexus at some point, will you?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I will have to speak to that now, your Honour; I was not going to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. The Appeals Chamber spoke to the issue of whether or not the acts charged had been committed in the context of an armed conflict. I believe that the Defence took the position in their pretrial brief that this was a preliminary finding, jurisdictional, and relates really to the question that Judge Stephen raised, and that is that it was done without the benefit of testimony. We had exhibits, of course, the Trial Chamber did, and those exhibits remained part of the record that went to the Appeals Chamber, but need we not now find that and what does that mean? Does it mean that the act committed has to be committed during the armed conflict -- I think that maybe the Defence's position -- or while the conflict is not going on but has begun and has not ended through a formal cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe that there is some law to suggest that, perhaps, for a year after a cease-fire they may still be under the protections of the Conventions. But in the brief that was submitted on this at an earlier stage, we had spoken to what the nexus was.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. Before we do that, Miss Hollis, you mentioned earlier in your argument that the evidence had shown that there were prisoners taken in JNA helicopters, transferred to Serbian prisons and subjected to the same treatment. I do not recall that being in the submission that you filed on internationality. It may be in there. I may have missed it. But in response to Judge Stephen's request, if you can find a transcript cite if it is not in there during the break, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, first of all, in relation to your question about the reference for the use of JNA helicopters on about 4th May, that is found in the testimony of Mr. Tihic at pages 441 to 451. In the written submissions on proof of international armed conflict, that same cite was given on page 3 at the bottom of the very first paragraph that ends there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Page 3, the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, the very first one, your Honour, where it starts out "BiH after May 19 1992". That includes the reference to Tihic at pages 441 to 446.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it also has been pointed out to me that I misspoke on something that there should be no question about and that is, of course, the attack on Kozarac was 24th May. I believe I said 23rd. I am correcting that for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As to your question about nexus, your Honour, in the Prosecutor's pretrial brief, at page 12 of that brief, we very briefly talk about the nexus. In that regard, we indicate that the nexus required between the commission of the crimes and the conflict, as described by the Appeals Chamber, is only a relationship between the conflict, not that the acts occurred in the midst of a battle. In that regard, your Honour, we would submit that the nexus requirement would be as follows, and that is that the person committing the grave breach need not be a member of the military forces to commit a grave breach, but in order to establish the necessary nexus, then the perpetrator must be operating in concert with and or in some way with the acceptance of the belligerent to the conflict. We suggest that means much more broadly than the military; the belligerent to the conflict in this regard is the FRY. A person could be acting in concert with and or with the acceptance of the belligerent either through their position in the police, in the political leadership or hierarchy in the military, as a paramilitary troop or even outside that if a person is operating under circumstances that lead you to believe they are operating with the acceptance of the belligerent. In this regard, we have this accused involved in the acts throughout opstina Prijedor to such a great extent that we suggest the only reasonable conclusion from that is that he was acting in concert with and or with the acceptance of the belligerent. We suggest it is too great a coincidence to be coincidence that the acts he was involved in were the very acts that were being carried out also by the police, by the military, were being ordered, sanctioned and involved in by the SDS leadership. If there are no other questions about international conflict or the protected status of the victims, I would now like to turn to the Article 5 common element, that is, the proof of widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population. There is extensive evidence in this record and that record proves beyond reasonable doubt that the attacks against non-Serbs in opstina Prijedor were widespread or systematic attacks against a civilian population. If you could also look at the Elmo, given uncertainties about the proof here as to how widespread or how systematic -- I think we are experiencing some technical difficulties, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Elmo needs to be turned on.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While they are working with that, your Honours, in regard to this proof ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Here we are, it is on.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- we believe that the evidence goes well beyond what we needed to prove in this case. We have, in fact, proven through the evidence that there was a widespread or systematic attack, not only against the civilian population in opstina Prijedor, but civilian populations throughout Bosnia. This chart indicates the areas for which you have evidence indicating attacks against civilian populations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: This is an existing Exhibit, is it?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour. This is a demonstrative aid for this argument. Certainly it will be available. We can see here how truly widespread the attacks were, and the evidence about the attacks show how truly systematic these attacks were. We submit in this case it would have been sufficient to prove widespread or systematic attacks only within opstina Prijedor, and in fact we have done that as well. If you would look again, this is evidence given to you by the many witnesses you have seen about the widespread nature of the attacks, the systematic nature of the attacks, and you will recall that in summary what the witnesses told you was basically the following. This is throughout Bosnia and in opstina Prijedor. Witnesses told you that at some point there came into existence a shadow government in their area; that at some point there had been brought into existence these SAOs, as we call them, these Serbian autonomous regions, that were set up by the Bosnian Serbs. When it became apparent that they would not be able to remain within Yugoslavia by the vote, they began to set those up. They set up parallel governments at that time, shadow governments. Then once that was all in place, they began working with the JNA and others to be sure to arm the local population of Serbs. They began to take actions to cut off the Muslims and the Croats from basically being a part of that area, from having any say in that area. They also in different areas actually took over the opstina, as they did in Prijedor. In Prijedor, they were able, because it was so well planned, to do it without a shot being fired. But these were concerted actions between the military, the police, the SDS leadership. They told you that what would happen. Azra Blazevic told you that when the blockade came into effect around Kozarac they knew what was going to happen. Why did she say that? Because they had seen it happen in Croatia. They knew that it had happened in other parts of Bosnia. What happened? They isolate the area. While they are isolating the area, they bring in weaponry. Witnesses told you about helicopters at night bringing weapons in. They told you about seeing the artillery being moved in place throughout the opstina. The Serbs more and more armed with the modern weapons. Serbs being made parts of either the military or Serb TO units. So, they bring in the weaponry, they isolate the area, blockades, checkpoints prior to the blockades where they check the non-Serbs going through and sometimes do not allow them to pass or harass them. They at some point decide they can no longer work at their jobs, though to be sure they know where they are, they have them show up for work though they cannot perform duties. They take over the police. You heard the evidence about the non-Serbs being forced to either sign allegiance to Republika Srpska or to leave the police. Most of them left. Then they isolate the area they are about to attack, as they did in Kozarac. They did that with a blockade. Not just the Prosecution witnesses, but Ljubo Tadic told you that the blockade was such that even he could not get in after the blockade was set up, although somehow the accused managed to get out. So, they set up a blockade of the area and then they attack the area, usually with very, very heavy shelling. Again this is from weaponry that belonged to the JNA that was left in place for them. Then after the attack, what did they do? In all these areas they go in, they round up the population and they move the population out and, typically, they separate out the service aged men from the women, the children and the elderly. In some instances, that separate out all the men from the women and children, leaving the women and the children then more vulnerable to attacks on them. They send off the men to camps. Very often they send off the women to camps as well or they allow them to remain for a time in the villages. It follows on from there. Widespread or systematic, both within the opstina and outside the opstina. That has certainly been proven by all the evidence. This widespread or systematic attack took place in the opstina and the accused acts in the opstina or acts that he knew was in furtherance of this widespread or systematic attack. Everything that he did paralleled what everybody else was doing. Everything that he did was to achieve the goals of this widespread or systematic attack. That is, to attack non-Serbs, to force them through a variety of means to leave the area. That included killing some of them, beating them savagely, depriving them of their homes, depriving them of their property, making it impossible for them to continue to live in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding the attack, is there any evidence that the accused knew about the attack?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have evidence that puts him there on the night of 24th firing a flare that illuminates the area around the hospital, and that shortly thereafter there is shelling that recommences near the hospital. In fact, the hospital is hit that night. Azra Blazevic told you about the hospital being hit. Witness Q told you about seeing the accused. In addition to that, we have something that perhaps on its own would be coincidence but, given the overall circumstances, we suggest is not coincidence, and that is that the accused does, in fact, leave, according to the evidence, Kozarac on 23rd. We suggest, in part, that is because he knows what is going to happen on 24th and needs to clarify what his involvement will be. We also have evidence of him being at Keraterm in police uniform, although that is later clarified to mean camouflage top, on 26th when, from the evidence we know, there had been a negotiated agreement that the non-Serbs in Kozarac would surrender on that morning. We have a witness seeing him in Keraterm that morning around 10 o'clock or after in his camouflage uniform. We suggest that is because he was aware that this surrender had been agreed upon and was prepared to go back into Kozarac at this time to participate in the round-up and the transport of these now captured peoples to camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you ask you something here? This seems to me to go both to the question of nexus and also to that of widespread or systematic. One might assume from the evidence that the overall plan, of which you say he was part because his actions were parallel with it, and also which is material because to know what the plan was overall assists one with the nexus question. One might assume from the evidence that the overall plan, as far as Kozarac was concerned, was its erasing from the face of the countryside, the destruction of the houses and leaving it as a ghost city, as it were; yet all he did seemed to be pointing in a quite different direction, the reconstruction of Kozarac. I mean, even the fact that he allows his brother to start a business in Kozarac just a few weeks before the attack certainly does not suggest that he thought that Kozarac was going to become a ghost town. What do you say to all of that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe that, in fact, the plan was to remove the non-Serbs from Kozarac and that was going to involve some damage to the town, to basically make it impossible for them to live there and that was going to involve some damage to the town. I do not know that the overall plan was to erase it from the earth. I believe there has been testimony from Azra Blazevic and others who talked about the fact that the shelling of the town certainly resulted in damage and there were fires as the people were being rounded up and taken away. If you recall, I believe she tells you that after she was taken to Trnopolje, there were two occasions she came back to Kozarac. The second occasion was when there was some damage and that on the subsequent occasion it had been, as you say, virtually erased. I believe what happened is that the activities there went somewhat beyond what the plan may have been. So I do not believe that is inconsistent with what we have here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Your map 1, which you are submitting as an aid which is acceptable, and your map 2 are somewhat different. Map 1, if I recall, covers more than the evidence that we received during the trial. It goes all the way down to Mostar. Map 2, though, covers less than the evidence that we received. If I remember correctly, when the map was on the Elmo, it did not go as far as Sanski Most, I think, and Bijeljina, was it ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Bijeljina, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- which is further east and south, I think. If we can see it again? The maps are helpful, except that this is the first one. Of course, we did not have evidence that dealt with all of this, did we?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you see Bijeljina appear. The evidence that was put in, either through experts or through fact witnesses, talked about all of these areas. You will recall that we had evidence from Mr. Vulliamy who, in his capacity as a journalist, visited many areas in Bosnia and talked to you about ethnic cleansing or widespread or systematic attacks that had occurred there, and also Mr. Doko. Both of them talk about Mostar. So this has been pulled from references made throughout the transcripts, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Doko was from Bosanski Samac maybe, was he? Somewhere up there, as I recall OK. That is fine.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As for the second one, your Honour, again we have attempted to go back and to pull out testimony that talked about all of these different areas.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But that is in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is only opstina Prijedor. It was our contention that the proof of the widespread or systematic attack in the opstina itself would be sufficient, but we have gone beyond that in the proof.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is there another question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Just a specific question, Miss Hollis: I refer particularly to charge No. 9 relating to serious injury, cruel and inhumane treatment, and to the incident where the accused was supposed to have discharged the contents of a fire extinguisher into the mouth of a person in a wheelbarrow. Can a person be guilty of cruel and inhumane acts to a dead body?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is certainly the issue in that charge. The position that we take on this is, as far as cruel treatment is concerned, you would not be able to prove that if it is a dead body because of the requirement for cruel treatment that you have injury, great injury or suffering inflicted, and if a person is dead, you could not. As far as other inhumane acts, your Honour, we would suggest that even if you were to conclude that the person in the wheelbarrow was dead, that certainly a beaten, battered person who has died in a wheelbarrow, discharging, shoving a hose into his mouth, could constitute other inhumane acts, that would certainly be an attack upon that person's dignity even though he is a dead person. But we do not believe that, if you conclude that the victim is dead, there could be a finding of guilty of either serious bodily harm or great suffering or of cruel treatment. The issue would boil down to the Article 5 charge of other inhumane acts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think the problem with that count, one of the problems, is that the witness Mr. Grozdanic testified in answer to a question from one of the counsel that he did not know whether the witness was alive or dead, I think.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is exactly right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we do not know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is what raises the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What do we do with that? I may be getting you ahead of yourself and, if so, you can address it at a later time, if you wish. Are you going to discuss the various counts ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I can handle it now, your Honour, if you wish. That is no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Tell me. We do not know whether he is dead or alive from the testimony. That is our problem.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As we see it from the testimony, there is no testimony that he is alive; there is no testimony that he is dead. A reasonable inference from the accused's acts could be that the person, and we believe there is a reasonable inference, is alive and he is shoving this into his mouth to inflict further pain or suffering on this individual or to commit an inhumane act upon him. If you determine that the evidence is insufficient to show that the person is alive, and I believe, as I said, that the charge of the Article 2 violation, great suffering and serious injury, you would have to find the person is alive. The Article 3 charge, cruel treatment, you would have to find the person is alive. If you find that the evidence does not prove that beyond a reasonable doubt, then you must look at inhumane acts. So, for purposes of the Article 2 and Article 3 charges, I believe you would have to make a determination about whether he was alive or dead. Quite honestly, looking at the evidence, I think it would be difficult to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that he is alive. I think there is a reasonable inference there and an argument to be made, but I think that there is a very difficult factual determination for you to make. If you conclude the proof does not establish that beyond a reasonable doubt, then the issue remains inhumane acts under Article 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You do not have to be a living member of humanity to be the victim of inhumane acts.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would suggest not, your Honour, but there are things that can be done to corpses that would be an inhumane act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis the corpse?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, because of philosophical attitudes towards what happens to you when you die, and also because of the standards we expect of respect for human beings even after the moment that they cease to live.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With respect to widespread or systematic, does the accused need actual knowledge that his acts were part of a widespread or systematic attack in order to incur liability or is it sufficient if he should have known?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course, we have under 7(3) the idea that a person in a position or superior position can be found guilty for either did know or should have known, but I would suggest that here either standard would be appropriate; that if your act is in such concert with the widespread or systematic attack that you reasonably should have known, then you could hold a person liable. I think this evidence, though, looking at the evidence itself and all reasonable inferences to be drawn from that evidence, in fact, the evidence proves that the accused knew that his participation here was in furtherance of this widespread or systematic attack.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Also need there be State involvement to establish a crime against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To the extent it has to be a widespread action or a systematic action, then at least you have to have, I believe, some group that is planning this widespread action or this systematic action, whether that group has to be a State entity or some other organised entity. I would suggest it does not have to be state entity, but it has to be some sort of group that is conducting this in some sort of concert of action. So there does have to be an organised entity somewhere in that. For example, if you were to conclude that Republika Srpska or the SDS officials in opstina Prijedor were the ones who were carrying out this widespread or systematic attack, I believe that is sufficient. Republika Srpska is not a State, is not an independent nation of the world, but I believe that would be sufficient proof. Also, again referring to our pretrial motion, on pages 48 and 49 we discuss crimes against humanity being committed by or on behalf of entities exercising de facto control over a particular territory. So again you certainly do not need recognition as an independent state. If you have an entity that is exercising de facto control over an area, that would be sufficient for crimes against humanity as well. Again, your Honours, that was in our pretrial brief and that was pages 48 and 49 where we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Article 5, Crimes against Humanity, in our Statute requires that it be directed against a civilian population. If the civilian population is part of a resistance group, particularly with reference to the Barbie case, does that change the protection that is afforded a civilian? So if you could tell me, what do you mean by a civilian population or what do you think that the Statute in Article 5 means by civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What we believe it means, your Honour, is that the population as being attacked is a population that is predominantly civilian, that it is not a fortified military camp, that it is not a fortified police area where the police are part of the belligerent force that is carrying out attacks, but that, rather, it is the civilian community. It could be that in this regard we also get into considerations of were there military targets within a town, because you can have a civilian community that would have military targets; those military targets would be subject to attack. Then the issue would become one of proportionality. But especially today we have in many civilian communities military targets. We have communication centres that would be military targets. We suggest, though, that for purposes of the attacks that were carried out through opstina Prijedor, we are not talking about such attacks against military targets, because if you think about Kozarac, for example, what were the military targets? The hospital was not a military target. What was the one thing that, based on the evidence, could potentially have been a military target? That was, perhaps, where the TO supposedly had its weaponry and headquarters and that was at the old school. But were the attacks carried out in such a fashion that you can say what they were really trying to do was to hit this one target, or was it carried out so that what you say is what they were really trying to do was to attack the civilian population of this town? We believe that the evidence here clearly shows what they were really trying to do was attack the civilian population of this town. Again, your Honour, for your assistance, we refer you back to the pretrial brief, and again at pages 45, 46 over to 47 where we talk about what it means to say "civilian". In regard to the widespread or systematic nature of these attacks, one of the things that we found (and the evidence proves) is that they included terror tactics such as killings, rapes and tortures. These were used and these were condoned by the military, by the police, by paramilitary groups, by local Serb Territorial Defence units and certainly by the SDS leaders in the area. The terror of these attacks served to intimidate and discourage resistance and to compel non-Serbs to leave the area which was the overall aim. During the attacks or shortly following, the non-Serb cultural and religious symbols such as mosques were destroyed. Non-Serb businesses and houses were plundered, looted and destroyed. The camps that existed were also part of this plan and again the camps were run by the military, by the police. Sometimes, as at Omarska, you will note you had both the military and the police carrying out various functions at the camp. The military, at least on the outer areas, performing guard duties. You have heard evidence from a Defence witness that those duties were to protect the inmates from the people outside. We suggest it was to make sure that none of those prisoners were able to leave the area. But these camps were all established in conjunction with this overall plan. The guards at these camps wore a variety of uniforms. You would have police uniforms, you would have camouflage uniforms. All of these camps allowed in visitors who were allowed to basically do what they wished with the inmates there -- all of this in furtherance of the overall plan that existed. In regard to this overall plan, opstina Prijedor was very significant because it was strategically placed in a corridor that was linking the Serb dominated area in Croatia with Serbia and Montenegro. They wanted to keep open this ability to be in touch with and to bring in the Croatian Serbs into this larger area so they needed opstina Prijedor. As you recall before the war, the population of Prijedor was almost evenly divided between Muslims and Serbs and there were some Croats.
