As an indication of what the plan was in opstina Prijedor, you will recall the evidence that by June 1993 of the nearly 50,000 Muslims living in opstina Prijedor, all but 6,000 of those had either fled, been killed or forcibly transferred. That is certainly strong evidence of what the plan was here. In opstina Prijedor, also you found that the SDS and the military and other military and police forces followed the same pattern that I discussed before, that is, they acted in concert. The JNA was used primarily to secure areas or for the heavy weaponry that was required to go in and shell the areas. The checkpoint incident at Hambarine was used as a reason to conduct the attacks on Hambarine and is a reason to basically kick off the following attacks in the opstina. The Muslims and Croats who survived the artillery bombardments and the infantry and mechanized attacks were then rounded up by the military and police forces and brought to these camps after they had been segregated and singled out at collection points. On occasions, lists were seen to be used to identify certain people. Those people were subjected to special treatment, very often resulting in death, almost always resulting in severe beatings. This cleansing, this forced removal of non-Serbs continued for several months. Cultural monuments and property of the Muslims were destroyed. Much of the personal and business property was plundered and looted. At the camps you received evidence of the horrific conditions that existed there. All of this was part of this overall widespread or systematic attack. As for Kozarac, Kozarac was also strategically placed within Prijedor. As you recall, it sat on the new highway going from Prijedor to Banja Luka, and from that area Banja Luka on towards Serbia and from Prijedor on up to the border. Kozarac was a very small town. It was very pleasant. If you would look at the Elmo, you will recall the Exhibit introduced showing what Kozarac was like before these attacks began. The overall area, as you recall, was an area of about 24,000 people, but Kozarac itself, the town, was a fairly small town -- about 4,000 people lived there -- and it had a very, very small main business area with Marsala Tita being the main business street that ran through the town. It was an area that boasted many cafes. It was a very pleasant area. It was a tourist area. It was an area that, for a variety of reasons, the cleansing of which was an integral part of the plan in opstina Prijedor. Looking at all of the evidence before you, the evidence of record proves beyond reasonable doubt the existence of both a widespread attack and a systematic attack, although we submit we need only prove one or the other, widespread or systematic, but in fact the evidence here proves both. Your Honours, in regard to the evidence that I have discussed ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you go on, just as to the difference, if I may, because the Defence takes the position, at least in the pretrial brief, that you do have to show widespread and systematic. You say "widespread or systematic". What does "systematic" mean? Are you referring to the way that the attacks were co-ordinated, that they occurred in other locations even outside of the Prijedor? Tell me?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the meaning of "systematic"?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I believe "widespread" just talks about the scope of the attacks, and "systematic" talks about when you look at them you can see that there is a plan here, an overall purpose to these attacks themselves. They are planned. They are a deliberative process. They are not an accidental process here, an accidental process there. That is what I mean when we talk about "systematic", that they are carried out in a planned, organised, deliberate sort of way to achieve an overall purpose. Either one of those, we suggest, are sufficient because either one of those impacts upon the reason that we have crimes against humanity as crimes in the first place. First of all, if you have a group being involved over a large area with carrying out a variety of offences against another group, that is a reason that we should say this is not allowed. This transcends a national jurisdiction. This becomes an international matter of certain. By the same token, if you have one group in a very systematic, deliberate fashion attacking another group, even though it may be in a smaller area, again this is something the international community steps in and says: No, we will not allow that and that sort of deliberativeness, that sort of planning, is what brings it out of the sphere of a national jurisdiction and brings it to the level of international concern and an International Tribunal. So that we believe that indeed as it is written it is in the disjunctive. It is "or" because either of those types of acts bring it within the gamut of crimes against humanity. If we could again refer you to the pretrial brief, on page 48 we also talk about factors that are considered in looking at both the scale of the acts and the deliberate nature of the acts. Certainly "widespread" could be something of an indicia of systematic. When you see that the same types of things are occurring over a large area, again that would be another indicia of the fact that it is a systematic attack. Your Honours, we have provided you in writing with a summary of what we believe is significant evidence, although again not all the evidence, and we have a great many references to the transcript in that summary we provided. We have also for your assistance, if you wish, compiled extracts of the cites that were referenced in the summary. If you wish that, we have that available and we will make it available to you. It may assist you without having to look through the entire transcript for these cites.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is for widespread or systematic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is for both international armed conflict, your Honour, and widespread or systematic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I just quickly looked again at your submission on widespread or systematic and I do not see the cite to the reduction of the Muslim population in Prijedor from 50,000 to 6,000.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there was testimony about that with Greve and there was also an Exhibit that was introduced that showed basically who we are, and that was from the paper in Prijedor showing the population based on ethnic groups. I believe that was a 1993 study. I will make a note of that and at a later time, your Honour, tell you what that Exhibit number was. If there are no further questions about the common elements, I would like for a moment to address theories of liability under 7(1). Again we have provided you with a legal memorandum talking about various theories of liability and how we believe 7(1) should be interpreted. It is, of course, true that we must go beyond the common elements and prove that the accused by his actions incurred individual criminal liability. It is article 7(1) that gives us the boundaries of that individual liability. We suggest that looking at Article 7(1) it draws those boundaries very widely indeed. The language of Article 7(1) and the Secretary General's comments reflect the modern trend to move away from very technical definitions about the degree of culpability, and instead move us to focus on whether the accused's actions in any way incurred criminal liability. Statutory language such as to encompass all forms of liability, the relative degree of culpability, is a matter for sentencing should you reach findings of guilt. In the findings phase the issue should be the accused's act render him liable under any theory of liability, not that the Prosecution must select a theory and then once that theory is selected, all other theories are foreclosed. The Prosecution charging in this case is consistent with the Secretary General's comments defining the scope of liability, that is, that through his acts the accused participated in the crimes alleged. The Secretary General's comments indicate that any participation which contributes to the preparation or commission of offences renders him individually liable. To assist you in your deliberations in the written submissions we have suggested various bases for liability, but those suggestions are in no way limiting. Depending on your assessment of the evidence and the accused's acts, you may have different views of liability. Should you find the evidence proves the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt under any of the theories of liability covered by Article 7(1), then the Prosecution has met its burden and the accused should be convicted. The Memorandum of law that we provide you gives examples of how to define some of the terms that we find in the Statute. The Statute puts the emphasis where it does belong, and that is: did the accused through his knowing actions contribute in any way to the commission of the charged offences? He can do that in a number of ways. He can do that by knowingly aiding and abetting or otherwise assisting in the commission of the offences. He can do that by in any manner whatsoever being engaged in the operation of one of the camps. The Mauthausen case talks about that. In this case you have evidence of this accused regularly visiting the camps in opstina Prijedor. He is seen there by people on numerous occasions. He is seen in Keraterm. He is seen in Omarska. He is seen in Trnopolje. Regularly seen there, especially in Omarska, the worst of all of these camps, a camp which can only be described as a death camp, a camp which had no lawful reason for existing. He can also be found guilty by the evidence that shows him connected with the commission of the offences. Under Australian law the most marginal act of assistance or encouragement would amount to an act of complicity in the crime. The accused's presence as a member of a group that is furthering the persecution of non-Serbs certainly assists and encourages that crime. This presence at scenes where prisoners were being beaten renders him there available to assist, reinforces the control over the victim, prevents the victim from acting on any thoughts the victim may have of fleeing the scene, even if that flight would only take him away from the immediate vicinity of the crime. Certainly, presence among a group when these crimes are being committed renders him individually liable for these crimes. Aiding and abetting includes all acts of assistance by word, by acts, by encouragement, support or again by presence. You have received evidence in this case from a number of people who told you that they had seen the accused at the camps in the opstina. They did not see him beating anyone, killing anyone. They saw him there either with camp personnel or alone, but there. The significance of those repetitive sightings must be evaluated in the context of what happened at those camps, and what the accused's other activities were during the time period. If the presence is intended to aid, to support or to encourage the chief factors, liability is incurred. Repetitive presence at a camp such as Omarska transforms passive presence into presence that is pregnant with meaning, and can be the basis for determination that it is not mere presence but rather significant presence. When you view the sightings that these witnesses have talked about in context, which you must do to determine the significance of those sightings, you must view them with the surrounding circumstances in the light of everything you know. When you view those sightings in that context, they become significant presence, pregnant with meaning, not mere presence and signify the accused's criminal participation in the ongoing persecution that occurred in opstina Prijedor during the time period alleged. If there are no questions about theories of liability, I would like to move on to knowledge of the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have a few questions. Looking at the material that you submitted it appears that some countries treat someone who has aided or abetted as an accessory and other countries, most notably the United States, would treat that person as a principal. We of course will be applying not national laws or national case law. We will be applying international humanitarian law. From looking at the Statute, of course, it must rise to the level of customary international law. So, can you tell me whether there is any support within the notion of customary international law that an accomplice would be treated as a principal, or does it make any difference? I think from the very first statement you made you are saying, if I understand you correctly, that we decide the culpability and then -- you did not say this but I gather you meant -- whether we treat the accused, should we find him guilty, as an accessory or as a principal that is matter for sentencing. So need we look for some support in customary international law that an accessory is treated as a principal or is it enough for us to determine that there is culpability and then handle it at the time sentencing?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that it is enough to determine there is culpability. In that regard I also believe that you are guided by the language of Article 7(1) itself which is very broad in its scope. Once you determine that within the reasonable definitions of the words used in that Article the accused is culpable, then the findings of guilty would be entered. So that it would not matter if you determine that his culpability in some crime perhaps was as a chief actor, principal in the first degree. In other instances it was as an aider and abettor, perhaps a principal in the second degree in some jurisdictions. In others perhaps it is an accessory which in some jurisdictions an "accessory" means accessory after the fact, the crime is committed, but still that is a theory of criminal liability. It does not really matter which one of those theories, or if you go beyond to the thought of complicity which may not be specifically embodied in those theories, it simply is that at the finding stage interpreting the language of 7(1) you find culpability proven beyond a reasonable doubt that is sufficient for a finding of guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With respect to the intent requirement, is it necessary that we find that the accused intended to further the commission of an illegal act, or only that he intended to commit an action that had the effect of furthering an illegal act?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Certainly if we look at Article 5, I believe the elements of proof that we submitted to you was that he committed an act and that it was unlawful. I think you are going to have to determine that the accused had some criminal mens rea or you cannot find him guilty. But there are various theories for establishing criminal mens rea as well. Did it have to be an overtly expressed intent?. No, I do not believe so and I do not believe any jurisdiction really requires that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose what I was thinking about is, let us suppose that there are a number of acts that are committed and there is evidence that the accused directly was involved in some of those acts, and that the acts were committed over a short period of time so that they could be interpreted as being part of the same transaction, using that word loosely, and that for some of the acts, as I said, there is evidence that the accused was actively involved and committed the acts, for another act, however, the only evidence is that he was there; can his presence then be interpreted as furthering the commission of the illegal act and, thus, he would be liable either as an accessory or as principal, depending on how we would treat those different concepts?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it would and I think we have two different issues here, perhaps. No. 1 is, if you have a single transaction and the accused is involved in certain discrete parts of that same single transaction, unless he does something affirmatively and decisively to remove himself from that single transaction, he is guilty of the entire criminal enterprise, the entire ongoing transaction. Secondly, as to presence, his presence there under those circumstances, his continued presence after he has participated, I would suggest, certainly is not mere presence but again is very significant presence and would be such as to indicate that he continues to participate by being there, ready to render assistance or encouragement for the discrete portions of that transaction in which he is not directly involved. So, yes, I believe there would be criminal liability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding this Mauthausen case that you cited on page 12 of your submission, there the persons charged were, you say, more than senior staff. Yes, in the Dachau case, they were all staff members at the camp; in the Mauthausen they were not. Did that court then find that the mere presence was sufficient to make a person aware of this common design and hold them culpable just by being present at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think the indication there was that it was not mere presence. I think that is the issue that we have to deal with. If it is mere presence, then I do not believe criminal liability attaches. It is the mere qualification that makes it not criminal liability. So were you to find mere presence anywhere, then you would not find criminal liability. Presence, however, given the circumstances of what is going on around you, given a camp which its only objective can be to commit crimes against persons, that it is an unlawful operation, the camp itself, then presence at that camp, especially in the context of an ongoing crime there, is not mere presence; it is, in fact, presence that is significant presence. In addition to that, when you look at the facts as we have them here, where you have repetitive presence at this camp, then you cannot really argue that this is mere presence, accidental presence -- went to the camp one day, did not know what was going on at the camp, did not know who was at the camp, perhaps, did not even know there was a camp there, stumbled upon it, left the camp, never returned -- but repetitive presence there, that is something that transforms presence into something meaningful, presence there while the atrocities were being committed, part of those atrocities you have taken part in, that makes it meaningful presence, presence there on other occasions when you were not just present, if you will, but you were there committing other crimes, given all those circumstances, that transforms that presence during this transaction, during a portion of this transaction, into a criminal presence, a presence for which you have individual criminal liability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Also you indicate on page 11 of your submission that the cases that you cite (and those are World War II concentration camps) provide the most analogous factual comparison for many of the counts against the accused. You refer to this as a "more narrow common plan or scheme theory of individual criminal responsibility". Why do you say it is more narrow?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because we believe that 7(1) is broader in scope than the theory of individual liability as being part of a common plan or scheme. We believe that the language is much broader.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because we believe that a person acting in any of the ways that are set forth in 7(1), you would not even have to show acting in concert with others, common plan or scheme, at some point you are acting in concert with others. You do not have to have the agreement that is required for conspiracy, but you do have this concert of action. 7(1) is much broader than that, though, and would not require such group activities to render a person criminally liable.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you do not have to show that a group sat down and had a little meeting to decide what would be done? Instead, if they act together, then you are saying that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That would be a common scheme or plan, but we say that 7(1) is even broader than that. You do not have to put him in a group section where you can imply some sort of commonality of agreement or purpose. Your Honour, I am not sure what your break time will be for lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think we are ready to break now, as soon as we gather our papers together. We will stand in recess for an hour and a half, 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you start, can I raise one matter? I seem to find myself in a position that I do not really know what the boundaries of Republika Srpska were. I have enumerable maps as exhibits. None of them seem to actually show that. I realise that it is not a recognised Republic, but it would still be useful. Am I wrong? Is there a map that shows us that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe we can prepare a demonstrative aid that would assist you, your Honour. I do not have one at this time. There is not one in evidence ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- but if we may make a note of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my colleague Mr. Keegan points out that the Dayton Agreement map (which I believe you do have in evidence) may indicate to you the boundaries of this subentity within Bosnia that is known as Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Exhibit number of that map is Exhibit 181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one additional matter that was raised earlier and that was in regard to the census figure showing the remaining Muslims in opstina Prijedor as of 1993. That was Exhibit 123 and the newspaper article that discussed the census results was Exhibit 124. Those census results were part of an unofficial census; it was not just a newspaper estimate of the numbers. If there are no additional questions concerning the theories of liability, I would like to move now into a discussion of knowledge of the accused. It is, of course, true that no matter how broadly you define liability, the Prosecution must prove that it was the accused who committed the acts that render him criminally liable. In this case, we have called some 50 fact witnesses who testified as to the accused's involvement in the crimes alleged. Of those some 50 witnesses, all but four knew the accused before the Serb attacks began in opstina Prijedor. Four of them did not know him before but recognised him when shown a photographic lineup after the fact. All of those witnesses came into this courtroom, took an oath to tell you the truth and testified that they had seen the accused either committing crimes, ordering others to commit crimes or being present at camps which the Serbs created to forcibly detain and severely mistreat civilians. How was it that the great majority of these people knew this accused? The facts before you in this record make the explanation quite clear. The Tadic family was a very prominent family in Kozarac. The accused's father was a World War II hero who was known and respected by all. His wife had been a captive at the notorious Jasenovac prison camp and was also very well known. The accused grew up in the Tadic family home in the heart of the business street in Kozarac, and that was a very small area. He lived there most of his adult life as well, even after he married. He did for a short period live at another address in Kozarac, but that was not far away. Indeed, it was not far off the main street itself. He, no doubt, continued to be seen on the main street very often even when he lived at that other address. In the later years, the accused was in Libya but for less than a year. When he had the business in Croatia, he was not far away, perhaps 70 kilometres, maybe a two-hour drive. His family remained in Kozarac and, no doubt, he visited Kozarac very often. So the accused was a well-known, continuing presence in the Kozarac area. Kozarac, as I mentioned earlier, was a small town and he lived on the small main business street there. So he was seen by many as they came to Kozarac for their shopping, for their visiting, for their entertainment. Because he came from a well-known family and that notoriety rubs off on to the children of those parents, many people knew him because of his family. In addition, his brothers and he were also well-known as karateists. He taught boys karate and was to some of them an idol. They would watch him train or teach classes, or take classes from him. Students remember and recognise teachers or coaches or trainers, especially those whose talents they admire. Teachers or coaches, on the other hand, do not remember all or even most of their students. So it is not surprising or puzzling that Elvir Grozdanic would remember his trainer, the accused, but the accused would not have a clear memory of what Elvir Grozdanic looked like. There was one primary school for the Kozarac area and children from the surrounding area came to that school. They saw the accused when they came to school there. Some of them have told you they went to school with him there. The accused married a woman from the local area, the area of Vidovici. Some people living in that area, such as Senija Elkasovic, knew the accused both from Kozarac and also because others like her knew his wife Mira Tadic and saw the accused with her and learned more familiarity of him after he married her. The accused later opened a coffee bar in Kozarac at the end of 1990 or at the beginning of '91. His brother Ljubo told you that it was a popular bar frequented by many people in Kozarac and the surrounding area. People knew him from that as well. Emsud Velic told you that the accused displayed in that bar his karate trophies, photos and newspaper articles about him; further evidence of how people would be familiar with him. For very logical reasons, many people from the Kozarac area knew the accused to say "hello" to him in passing or just to recognise him when they saw him on the street or about in Kozarac. Many of those people came into this courtroom and testified to that effect. Hakija Elezovic's knowledge of the accused is perfectly consistent with the small town setting that was Kozarac. He knew of the accused, that is, knew his name for one reason because his son, Salih, knew the accused and would talk about Dule Tadic to his father, Hakija Elezovic. He also knew the accused because he had seen him when he went to Kozarac, but for sometime had no name to connect with that face. Then an incident provoked much public attention and comment, the incident involving the alleged threatening letter. It was a news item for those in the local area. Hakija was interested in that and, as a result, had someone point out this Dule Tadic who, it was rumoured, may have written the threatening letter to himself. When this Dule Tadic was pointed out to Mr. Elezovic, he realised that this was the man he had seen in passing in Kozarac for five or six years. So at that time he linked up the face with the name. That is the reasonable explanation for how he was able to recognise the man who beat him in Keraterm and beat him, his son and the others at Omarska. Some Prosecution witnesses, like Hakija or Azra Blazevic, knew the accused in passing. Others knew him very well. The recognition witnesses in the case all had sufficient knowledge of him to recognise him when they saw him. The 46 or so witnesses who were recognition witnesses had sufficient knowledge to recognise him. The Defence expert, Dr. Wagenaar, told you that if you know someone it takes less time to recognise them when you see them, to imprint that on your mind, and you can certainly do that in less than optimum conditions. As for the four identification witnesses in this case, that was Senad Muslimovic, Kasim Mesic, Witness R and Sead Halvadzic, Dr. Wagenaar told you these witnesses have additional significance to you. If you find credible their testimony that they saw the accused in Keraterm, Omarska and Jaskici, in the case of Zemka Sahbaz, that testimony places him there. To determine credibility of these witnesses, in addition to the factors I previously mentioned, it is necessary to determine whether the photo array and the procedures used were so grossly inadequate as to invalidate the identification. The procedures do not have to be perfect, but may not be so suggestive that you cannot trust the result. There were no such problems with the photo identifications used in this case. First, concerning the photo array that was used: Dr. Wagenaar himself okayed that photo array in his letter of 27th March 1996 which is Exhibit D90. Interestingly in that letter and before you in this courtroom, he mused about whether there were physical differences between either Yugoslavs and other people, or among Muslims, Serbs or Croats, which could render the choice of foils too suggestive. He did not give any scientific basis for these museings. Whether or not they may some day be proven to have a basis, there is no evidence before this court that this hypothetical concern has any foundation. To the extent it is a valid concern, the foils used in this photo array contain nine Yugoslavs. Dr. Wagenaar noted in his testimony that such a number would satisfy his concern on that possible issue. As for the procedure used, Dr. Wagenaar in his testimony gave you some of his rules concerning the procedure that should be followed. Many of those rules you are, no doubt, familiar with because many of those rules are common sense factors that should be considered when devising, showing and evaluating the results of any photographic lineup or other lineup. But, again what is of concern is gross deficiencies in those procedures. There were no gross deficiencies in the procedures used with the Prosecution witnesses. No witness was shown a single photo lineup or a photo lineup of only two or three individuals. The lineups that were shown contained either 11 or 13 photographs -- more than many jurisdictions would require as a minimum number. No witness was shown more than one photo lineup. No witness chose more than one person whom they identified as the accused. So no one had two or more chances at the identification. All the witnesses were certain about their choices. In total, the photo spread was shown to nine persons, including those who testified. Of those nine, eight identified the accused. The ninth did not pick anyone. Eight out of nine statistically tells you that the identifications were not based on chance. No witness took an unduly long time to look at the photo book. Dr. Wagenaar gave you his personal preference for a witness to be shown each photo only 30 seconds. Again, that appears to be a personal opinion of his. He did not indicate any scientific evidence to back up 30 seconds. When he contrasted that time, if you will recall, he contrasted it to a witness being allowed to spend hours looking at a photo book. In any event, the witnesses to whom the Tadic photo spread was shown took, on average, about three minutes to view the photo book. During the testimony it was stated that Senad Muslimovic seemed to know there was a trial going on. That, we suggest, does not imply that, contrary to his testimony, he had seen anything about the accused in the media. The circumstances would have led him to surmise that. He had been interviewed about the accused, then asked to take part in a photo lineup. A logical conclusion from that would be that there was an ongoing or upcoming trial or some proceeding in order for those prior interviews and then this photo lineup to have been conducted. Dr. Wagenaar told you that an identification witness must have sufficient time to form a good impression of the accused. The time it takes to do that may not be all that long, however. Because another important factor to consider when evaluating the photo identifications is that the human brain seems to be "hard wired" to recognise human faces and remember human faces. In that recognition and memory, it is not a discrete process whereby an individual looks at a face and memorises each discrete detail, but rather it is a global process in which the overall image is stored for memory. Of course, witnesses who knew the accused before seeing him at the camps would be able to recognise him very quickly and under much less than optimal conditions. As for distance and identification, Dr. Wagenaar postulated that a sighting within 15 metres is fine, no problems there, but that problems could begin after that distance. We suggest that is a very conservative estimate and that, in fact, people are able to see and recognise faces well beyond that distance, even those of us with eyes that have been looking at faces for some years now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question on that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was it Dr. Wagenaar's testimony regarding that point that that 15 metres problem was for persons who did not know the accused before or was it for both groups? I thought it was only for if they did not know him before, but I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: My recollection, your Honour, is that he was speaking in that context of identification. I would assume that distance becomes a problem at some point even for those who know him, but the 15 metres was again a distance within which you should have no difficulty recognising someone. He indicated that beyond that problems may start but did not indicate that there were problems immediately. It is just that then distance becomes a factor, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that for the four individuals who had indicated they did not know Mr. Tadic before?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe it was the identification witnesses, the four I had indicated, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you two questions? It is right, is it, that we have only heard from one person who administered to one witness a photospread?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Mr. Reid provided the information concerning the others, but he did not administer the test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But that was second-hand; he had been told it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The other thing is, do we know whether any other, apart from the eight, from evidence, were not shown photospreads and did not, for instance, make incorrect recognitions?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The evidence that you were given, your Honour, from Mr. Reid was that nine persons, total, had been shown the photospread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And no others?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And no others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Reid can testify to that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Paepen did testify regarding the one that there was non-recognition at first -- at least that is how I would characterise it -- but he is not the person who administered the photospread in the first instance. That is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did he administer it the first time?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought he was testifying about when he went back to her -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In fact, he did not go back to her, your Honour. That was his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Sorry, I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Another issue that Dr. Wagenaar talked to you about was the issue of facial hair. Dr. Wagenaar, you will recall, told you that if a witness saw an accused with facial hair and then was shown a picture of that accused without facial hair and could still recognise that accused, then that witness would not be guessing. In effect, by taking a witness who had seen the accused at the crime scene, the accused having facial hair, and then showing that witness a photo of an accused without facial hair, you are building, sort of, a test within a test, and indicated that the difference in that, from the viewing at the scene and the viewing in the photospread, in fact, made the test more difficult for the witnesses and indicated, as a matter of fact, that was why criminals often shave off their facial hair so that they can fool people about identity. He indicated that if people knew the accused, if they could recognise him, that whether they could remember he had facial hair or not was not really that significant to their overall identification or recognition. Another area that was discussed by Dr. Wagenaar was the effect of exposure to the accused's image in the media or elsewhere. The photospread identification, in the event that such other exposure was had, could then be based on seeing that image and not based on seeing the accused at the crime scene. Of course, if a witness saw the accused at the crime scene and then later saw an image of the accused on the television or in the media, that does not negate the first showing; it is simply for your decision-making here that that would be a factor to consider. That issue becomes a normal issue of assessing the believability of the witnesses. The issue of prior exposure has been addressed by the Defence in their cross-examination of identification witnesses. The witnesses have said that they had no prior exposure. They have explained why it is that they have not seen the accused's image in whatever area they are in. The explanations are very reasonable explanations. First of all, many of these witnesses are in areas where they do not understand the language so that their interest in the media is much less. Secondly, some of them do not have access to programmes that would show anything about the accused or this case. Because of where they live, it is simply not an item of great significance. Perhaps most importantly, however, the witnesses told you over and over again that they have been traumatized by their experiences in opstina Prijedor and they do not want to see these kinds of images. In fact, they try very consciously to stay away from them. That is not at all unreasonable to understand that traumatized people want to avoid seeing things that bring back all of the memories that are so painful and so difficult for them. That is what these witnesses have told you. There is no reasonable basis in record to conclude that the identification witnesses saw an image of the accused in the media such as to invalidate their identifications. The reasonable explanation for the evidence that was given by these some 50 fact witnesses in conjunction with the documentary evidence in this case is that the accused is guilty as charged. I would like now to turn to the counts themselves for a more in-depth discussion of the proof of each. In doing this, I will generally follow the counts in the order charged, but will vary on some occasions for a more chronological flow. When I do that, I will tell you that that is what I am doing. I would like first to turn to count 1 which is the count which alleges the accused took part in persecution of non-Serbs in opstina Prijedor from about 23rd May until about 31st December 1992. Of course, for that we have to prove that the accused participated in the commission of certain acts and that those acts were intended to harass, cause suffering or otherwise discriminate based on political, religious or racial grounds. Count 1 alleges that the Serb actions in opstina Prijedor from May through December 1992 constituted persecution against the non-Serbs in that opstina, and that the accused participated in that persecution. The evidence clearly establishes that. Virtually all the fact witnesses told you of their hamlets, villages, towns and cities being taken over by Serb forces always with some form of force, often with shelling. In Prijedor, the barrage was with tanks primarily because the firing needed to be more selective because great areas of Prijedor were going to be saved and used by the Serbs. What was the area in Prijedor that was devastated? The old town area which was inhabited predominantly, almost exclusively, by Muslims. The same witnesses told you that virtually all the non-Serbs from these hamlets, villages, towns and the city of Prijedor were forced from their homes, beaten, some killed, men separated from women and children, sent to camps where they were mistreated and then people were expelled from the area after being forced to sign forms giving over all their property and agreeing not to return. The campaign of terror included rapes both inside and outside the camp. Suada Ramic testified that she was raped in the Prijedor military barracks, at her apartment, at the Prijedor SUP and on multiple occasions as she was held prisoner in the Omarska camp. She also told you of women taken out of their rooms almost every night. The victims of all of this persecution -- Muslims and some Croats. The victimizers -- Serbs. Why were these people forced from their homes, beaten, killed and otherwise abused? The evidence tells you that it was because they were non-Serbs, in particular, they were Muslims. The curses directed at them almost in every instance were the derogatory terms for Muslims,"Balija", as directed towards the SDA leader, a Muslim, Alija Izetbegovic, "Fuck your Alija" was a very common curse directed at them, both religious and political motivations for that. The abuse directed against Croats was also for political reasons. You will recall the testimony of Husein Hodzic about the severe treatment of Silvio Saric, who was the HDZ leader in opstina Prijedor. What did he tell you about Mr. Saric's treatment? He told you that Mr. Saric's condition after he was called out was one of the worst of all the men that were going and coming back. He could not walk. The only signs of life were heavy breathing and he did appear to be able see. Mr. Saric died of his injuries a few days later. In addition, the abuse was directed against this group, these non-Serbs, as a way to rid them from the area in keeping with the historic goal of greater Serbia, to intimidate, coerce, forcibly disperse or liquidate the non-Serb population to ensure Serb control of the area. Vasif Gutic told you of hearing the Trnopolje Camp Commander, Kuruzovic, explain that the Serb plan was to reduce the number of Muslims in Prijedor to 10 per cent or less, and then at a later point indicated, well, perhaps that has dropped to two per cent or less. The abuse was directed against this group for religious reasons, as I have mentioned, the men who had crosses carved on their bodies. This was a consistent practice. Elvir Grozdanic told you the Serbs did that to him. Hase Icic told you that was done to men in his room when he first arrived in Omarska. In addition, the men were consistently forced to hold their fingers, their hands, in the three finger Serb salute. What was that? That is the way that those of Orthodox faith cross themselves. You will recall Ljubo Tadic on the film clip that was shown to you justifying what was done to the Muslims as a result of a holly war the Muslims directed against all Christians and, therefore, they retaliated. Clearly, the acts committed against this group were done for religious or political purposes. The evidence also proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused willingly took part in the persecution of non-Serbs during the time period alleged. Even before the events occurred in opstina Prijedor in 1992, the accused was, apparently, only superficially tolerant of Muslims. Sofia Tadic told you of the accused seeing his Muslim neighbours pass by and saying, "The balijas are going to the mosque". When Milosevic came to power, the accused intended to name his next child after him if that child were a boy. He made statements to the effect that Milosevic was the only real man, the only real politician, in Yugoslavia. With the rise of Serb nationalism the family became religious where before they had not been. The accused became more overtly nationalistic as the political parties and, in his own estimation, was one of the first SDS members in opstina Prijedor. He was a trusted member of the SDS who was given the task of organising the Serb plebiscite for Kozarac. He and his wife Mira held the plebiscite at the Serb church in Kozarac. He would have you believe that he held it there because he felt it was unfair to hold it in a private place. This supposed concern for fairness is hardly supported by the record, however. He obviously had no problems with the fairness of giving non-Serbs a differently worded ballot, one that hid the true objective of the vote.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I ask you a question on that, actually two questions? I may have forgotten the first question already. The second question is I think Mrs. Tadic testified that there were not two ballots, unless I am misunderstanding the testimony. Dr. Greve, though, testified that there were two ballots. Then my second question relates to whether or not Mr. Tadic, from your point of view, was responsible for the plebiscite or just that one polling place? There seems to have been some confusion. As I re-read Mr. Tadic's testimony, I did not quite understand what he was saying, but then I read Mrs. Tadic and I understood something and then, of course, looked at the work report and understood something else. So, from your point of view, what was Mr. Tadic's involvement and responsibility for the plebescite? Was it limited to the polling place in Vidovici and, secondly, were there two different coloured ballots?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have introduced, in fact, into evidence the ballots that were given, and that is Prosecution Exhibit 97, that showed the wording of the ballot for Serbs and the wording of the ballot for non-Serbs. The wording, we suggest, is significantly different. As to Mira Tadic's testimony on that particular point, if we could note that and check the transcript so that I do not misstate what she may have said? As to the last question about the voting at the Serb church, certainly the accused has tried to down play the importance of that polling station and did indicate that it was really just for people from Vidovici and that there were, I believe he indicated, seven houses in Vidovici. Kozarac itself was an overwhelmingly predominant Muslim area with very few Serbs there. We believe, it is our position, that the evidence shows that the polling place in Kozarac was not just for Vidovici but, rather, was for the larger area. The report for the results of the voting in the plebiscite that the accused prepared -- that is Prosecution Exhibit 147 -- shows that there were 102 registered voters who voted and that, in addition, there were 37 Serbs who voted on the strength of their identification cards, and I believe indicated that there were eleven non-Serbs who voted in the area as well. So, we are talking about 139 people. If that is from seven households, those are fairly large households. So our position is that, no, it was not just for Vidovici; it was for the Kozarac area. Again it was a predominantly Muslim area, but those Serbs who lived in that area voted at that polling place.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have read the work report and Mrs. Tadic's testimony regarding whether or not voters voted at the home of the Tadic's and, of course, their home was in Kozarac. I thought that the work report had said that Muslims had voted at their home, that Muslims voted at their home; Mrs. Tadic testified they did not. But again I am asking you something that you will have to check the transcript on.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But it is our understanding of the evidence that, in fact, the voting did take place at the Serb Orthodox church in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I heard in testimony, but then when I heard from Mr. Tadic that is what I heard and not in the church. I think Mr. Tadic said that it was in the yard, the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is something else we will note and check for you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But with respect to Muslims voting at the Tadic's home, if you will check the work report and testimony of Mrs. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I know that there is evidence that at some point there was, perhaps, a determination made that they would hold the voting at the home and then later that was changed to the Serb church, but we will check that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe it was held at the church or somewhere within the confines of the church, but it had to do with Muslims voting. Again I was re-reading this just to get a handle on what was the plebiscite about, who was responsible for it and whether it was done at the request of the President of the SDS in Prijedor and whether it was limited to Vidovici. I saw some confusion about that. If you will locate it for me, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you some questions about this? The first one, why do you say it is unfair to have two different printed forms? Of course, the accused has nothing to do with the forms that are used -- he was only a returning officer -- but why anyway would it be inappropriate to have two forms, one for Serbs and one for non-Serbs, when their voting really is directed to ascertaining what the Serbs want ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It would not be unfair ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- to have two different forms if they were worded the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But if they were worded differently -- but they are.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: They were worded very differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was perfectly obvious to everyone participating that different questions were being asked.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do not know that it was obvious to the non-Serbs that, in fact, the language was different. I do not know that is established in the evidence at all. The reason we believe that it was unfair is that the language for the non-Serbs was a much broader sort of language in keeping with a unified goal, one people, one nation; whereas the language for the Serbs was very clearly to keep the Serbs all together. That was the misleading nature of it which we believe could have led to a different vote had the non-Serbs been shown the exact same language as the Serbs were. That is why I characterised that as unfair. Certainly, the accused did not write the language. However, he must have been aware of the language. So the point I was making is that his supposed concern about fairness in polling places does not transform itself to concern about fairness with the different wording in the ballots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then the second thing is the significance of his role in relation to this plebiscite. He was, in effect, nothing more than a returning officer, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was a returning officer. However, the evidence in the case suggests that only those people who were very solidly loyal to the SDS cause and aims were given that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How many other SDS members were there in Kozarac? Do we know?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am not sure we have evidence on that. There were very few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very few members, presumably?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I presume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to this evidence, the evidence shows that the accused began to have more Serb nationalists at his cafe displaying nationalist clothing or badges; Goran Borovnica, Witness W and perhaps as many as 30 others on occasion. While there they would sing Serb nationalistic songs and some of them came into that area armed with weapons. Very often the three fingered Serb salute was shown -- again other indicia of the rising nationalism in the area of which this accused was part. Also prior to the Serb attacks that began in opstina Prijedor, the accused was forced to leave Sefik Sivac's cafe after the accused became involved in a heated political argument there. The accused indicated after that his knowledge and his support for what was about to happen. You will recall that Witness AA testified that the accused said there would be greater Serbia, it would be theirs, meaning the Serbs, and Muslims would not be there, there would be no place for Muslims there any more. The evidence also seems to indicate his foreknowledge of the Serb takeover of Prijedor. Nada Vlacina said that she saw the accused on 27th or 28th April and that he was on his way to pick up his wife and family who were staying in another area. When he testified, the accused claimed that he was surprised when his wife and family came back on that date. Is it not too great a coincidence that she came back immediately before the Serb takeover of power in opstina Prijedor which, of course, we know occurred on 30th? Why would she come back at that time? Because the accused, and very possibly she herself, knew that this takeover was going to happen, and that after that the Serbs would be firmly in control. Also she came back to Kozarac because very soon after they were going to Banja Luka, and it was in Banja Luka that the accused was mobilized on 4th May. The evidence in this case does prove that the accused was mobilized on 4th May when he received the certificate for his automatic weapon and 300 rounds of ammunition, which was twice the normal amount that would be issued. Certainly, even if he were not mobilized on that date, it would not allow him to escape criminal responsibility for his later acts. However, the evidence is such that it is clear that on that date he was mobilized. That did not mean he took up arms at that date and began shooting anyone, but on that date he was mobilized. We have the certificate showing that he was issued the weapon on that date. You have the Exhibit indicating that the mobilization, a general mobilization, occurred on that date. The accused is, understandably, trying to discount the certificate and has come up with several stories concerning it, ranging from "I do not know anything about it", which he told to the Germans, to "Well, I had two certificates, a legitimate one and this one, given to me by my brother Ljubo". Of course, he got rid of the legitimate one. He tells you he did not keep that one. The one found in his apartment was the one he tells you was false, the one showing the 4th May provision of the weapon and the ammunition in Banja Luka. His brother Ljubo tried to help the accused with this story, but they contradict each other as to when he gave the certificate to the accused. Ljubo said it was after the first trip to Kozarac around 1st or 2nd June. The accused said it was 4th May when his brother gave it to him. That is what he told you in his testimony. What the evidence shows is that it was on 4th May when he received this certificate and it was given to him by officials in Banja Luka. No doubt at that time in Banja Luka, which was the headquarters for the regional Crisis Staff and also for the Banja Luka Corps, it was determined what his role would be in the eventual takeover of Kozarac. He knew the town and the people. He was still a trusted person there. You will recall that Ljubo told that business was thriving up until just before the takeover there. The people were still treating him as part of the community so that he could return to Kozarac. He had a cafe there, he had a home there, he had a legitimate reason to be there and he could go back and keep an eye on what was happening there. That was an area of significant interest to the SDS to the events that were about to happen. He did that. He went back there. He continued to try to discourage Serbs from working with locals on joint security efforts. In fact, in his work report he denounces the Serbs who took part in those joint security efforts. When he was asked to take part in a last minute predominantly Muslim attempt to peacefully negotiate concerning the Serb demands that were made on Kozarac, he first had a private meeting with Simo Miskovic, the SDS President, before going to the group meeting. That was to tell Miskovic what was happening, what was going to come up in the group meeting and to talk with him about what the accused's role would be in that meeting. You may recall Kemal Susic testifying that after the meeting the accused told him, "Kemal, Kozarac will be shelled". Other indications of the accused's special status at this time are that both before the attack on Kozarac and in the few weeks after that attack, by the testimony of his own witnesses, the accused is able to move about at will throughout the opstina, throughout the Prijedor, Kozarac and Banja Luka area. He can travel back and forth between Kozarac and Banja Luka as he pleases. When the blockade is in a place a few days before the attack on Kozarac, he is still able to get through that blockade and he is still able to get to Banja Luka, though his brother Ljubo testified that for him, Ljubo, it would have been impossible for him to get to Kozarac. After he had participated in the attack on Kozarac and the subsequent cleansing, he is able to go in and out of Kozarac with no difficulty, even getting, in his own name, a certificate for 10 ten litres of petrol from the military in Lamovita during a time when petrol was strictly rationed. The local man, Timarac, was not the one who got the petrol; it was the accused who got the petrol. These are not activities of a person who is evading the call up. These are not the kind of activities such a person would be engaged in. These are the activities of a man who was fully integrated into the upcoming attacks and, therefore, would be allowed to engage in such activities. The accused's positions and activities after much of the cleansing had been accomplished proved his contributions towards that cleansing and his status as a trusted and loyal SDS nationalist. He became the primary person in Kozarac. He was the Secretary of the Local Commune, President of the Kozarac SDS, in charge of population resettlement in Kozarac, given the authority to re-establish civilian control, the representative to the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. Only a person who was absolutely loyal to the Serb people could hold such positions. It tells you that in Prosecution Exhibit 367(B) and Prosecution Exhibit 104. He wrote of some of those positions in his work report, Prosecution Exhibit 344, a document that tells you much about his orientation and goals. Of course, he did not include his crimes in this document which he intended to be provided to the media but he did boast of the activities that would be, on the surface at least, non-criminal, such as his efforts to give guns to Serbs, to prevent joint patrols and other such activities. During the latter half of 1992 and a part of 1993, he continued to benefit from his past contributions to the effort. He got permission to take over a cafe, the OK cafe. He was prepared to pay 20 deutschemarks a square metre for 50 square metres of space, so he was getting money from somewhere. He continued to live in the nice apartment in Prijedor. This is the man who committed the offences in opstina Prijedor. This is not the common man, the refugee, he would have you believe he was. This is the Serb nationalist who saw the persecution there as an opportunity to contribute to the Serb aim of ethnic dominance in the region and, at the same time, to enhance his own status in the area, particularly in Kozarac. He also is a man who is willing to use violence to get what he wants and to pay back those with whom he disagrees. Sofia Tadic told you that in her testimony. That is the man who committed the crimes alleged in this indictment. The indictment talks about, in count 1, various acts of persecution in several different places and also includes the substantive counts in the persecution. It talks about his persecution efforts in Kozarac. On 24th May 1992, Kozarac and the surrounding areas were shelled by Serbs forces. On 26th May, Muslims and Croats in the Kozarac area began to surrender. Did the accused commit persecution in Kozarac during the attack on the town in the forced expulsion of these civilians and the forced transfer of those civilians to camps? The accused himself told you that he was part of that persecution when he told Mirsad Blazevic the following September, "I liberated Kozarac and nothing leaves here over my dead body". Mirsad Blazevic heard him saying that, in fact, not to Mirsad, but to Serbs who were trying to remove property from his town, from Kozarac. The accused was not saying that to protect Muslim property until their return. The accused was saying that to exercise his ownership over the town from which he had helped expel the Muslims, a town he now began to see as his town, his reward after his efforts. If you would look at the Elmo for the sightings we are going to talk about, five witnesses corroborate that statement of the accused that he liberated Kozarac. Five witnesses testified concerning incidents in which the accused participated directly in ensuring the Serb capture and cleansing of Kozarac: Witness Q, Azra Blazevic, Nihad Seferovic, Meho Alic, Nasiha Klipic. The five witnesses had known the accused for nine years or more before seeing him take part in the persecution in Kozarac. Four of the five had known him most of their lives or most of his life. They all gave evidence of the accused's direct involvement in the actual military attack on Kozarac beginning with the shelling on 24th and in the subsequent forced expulsion of the civilian inhabitants from that area and in separating them to be sent to camps. He directly participated in this persecution. His actions in this area directly contributed to the larger persecution as well. Witness Q described for you how on a Sunday night, the first night of the shelling, the accused and Bosko Dragicevic fired a flare, illuminating the area around the hospital. This was about 8.00 or 9 p.m., not far from the hospital, and there was sufficient light, Witness Q told you, for him to be able to recognise the accused. Shortly after seeing the accused and Dragicevic jumping over a fence, Witness Q saw the flare fired from the direction in which the accused had gone, and not long after that shelling recommenced, primarily in the area of the hospital. There were injured people in the hospital that night, and Azra Blazevic told you that, in fact, the hospital that night was hit by shells. On the night and early morning of 25th and 26th May, the Muslims in Kozarac accepted terms of a surrender. It was arranged that a column would be formed the next morning with the police in the front of the column and that the column would go down Marsala Tita Street and surrender. The next morning the column did set off with the police in the front. Ermin Strikovic, who was in that column, told you that about one kilometre from Kozarac on the new Prijedor/Banja Luka road the police vehicle was pulled off and the other parts of the column then continued on. In Keraterm at this time, on 26th, Witness S testified that he saw the accused in the morning after 10.00 a.m. He testified that the accused was about 30 metres away from him, and was wearing what the witness described as the top part of a police uniform and then single coloured pants. Later in his testimony he described what he meant by the top part of the police uniform. He said it was similar to a camouflage uniform the special units of the JNA used to wear, the people who had special tasks in the woods, that it was a uniform that looks like the ground. Why was the accused there at Keraterm that morning? Because he knew that the town was surrendering and he was preparing to go to Kozarac to participate in that forced expulsion of the civilian population there. After he left Keraterm, he went to Kozarac and began participating in the forced expulsion and murder of Muslims in Kozarac and their being taken to the detention camps. This was a busy period of time for the Serbs as they were rounding up people, separating them out and moving them off to camps. The accused was involved in all aspects of this activity and was seen at Kozarac, Keraterm and Omarska during those first days after the attack. In Kozarac, Armin Mujcic saw the accused and Goran Borovnica on a tank in the town during the day. The accused was getting off the tank. Armin Mujcic told you that when a young boy approached the accused, he saw the accused slap the boy. Azra Blazevic, who knew the accused previously as well, saw the accused crossing the road at the triangle area, crossing the road toward the school. She saw the accused just after a man had been called out of her group and he had been called out by a name by an unknown soldier. She told you that the accused at that time was in uniform and had a weapon in one hand with his hand raised as though he were greeting someone or calling to someone. Meho Alic told you that he saw the accused on 26th at the Limenka bus stop where men were being separated from women and children. The accused was passing by a bus. Those activities on the part of the accused described by those three witnesses constitutes participation in this persecution. The people who were being forced to leave their homes were being forced to do so because they were non-Serbs, for the most part Muslims. Again the names they were being called reinforces this, the derogatory names for Muslims. The accused's presence was effecting the persecution, aiding and abetting the larger persecution offence and encouraging the offence. To the extent you believe these three witnesses testify about the accused's presence only, it is not mere presence, it is significant presence, and must be considered in the context, not just of Kozarac on that day, but of the overall circumstances that you know about this accused. Nihad Seferovic saw the accused the day Kozarac surrendered. He testified that he thinks that it was Tuesday that he saw the accused. He saw the accused and other Serbs, including Goran Borovnica, with six Muslim policemen lined up at the Serb church. The policemen were Edin Besic, Ekrem Besic, Emir Karabasic, Osman, who was the Commander of a police unit, and others that the witness did not name. The accused stabbed both Osman and Edin Besic in the throat and body. Nihad saw this from a position across the street during the day time. Hamdija Kahrimanovic told that you when he was finally released from the camps and allowed to go to Prijedor, the Chief of Police there, Simo Drljaca, confirmed that Osman was dead saying, "Look what you people have done, you have murdered him". On Wednesday, 27th May, in the afternoon, probably between 12.00 and 2.30 p.m., witness S again saw the accused in Keraterm, this time not in the morning but in the afternoon. The accused was wearing the same type of clothing, but this time when the witness saw him it was from some 20 metres away and the accused had his foot on a police vehicle. That same day in the afternoon, Nasiha Klipic also saw the accused as she came from Brdjani with others to surrender. As the column moved on the new Prijedor Banja Luka road in the direction of Prijedor, she saw a Golf police car. She saw Brane Bolta driving a car and she saw the accused and Goran Borovnica in the car. The car was coming from the direction of Prijedor. When the column reached the Kozarusa bus station, the accused, Goran Borovnica and other Serbs were separating men from 15 to 65 years of age from their wives, mothers and children. The accused was asking, "Where do I take these? Where do these go?" Shouting at people, "Hey, you?" The column of people surrendering and being separated were unarmed Muslims. The elderly women and children were taken to Trnopolje camp. The men were being separated to be taken to either Keraterm or Omarska. By all these acts, the accused was committing or aiding and abetting in harassing, causing suffering to and discrimination against non-Serbs, predominantly Muslims, based on political and religious grounds. The accused's evidence does not give him an alibi for these incidents. His duties with the traffic police had not yet begun. The testimony of Witness X does not assist him. Even if you believe that she independently remembers that the accused came to her home on 23rd May, she says that he left the next day, 24th May. The evidence shows how freely the accused moved about the area. So, even if you believe she could remember the dates independently, her testimony does not give him an alibi for the night of 24th. Her testimony is suspect in that regard. How does she remember it was the evening of 23rd May when the accused came? What was the significance of that date that makes her remember? She was not shelled the next day. She was not even close enough to hear or see the shelling. No doubt the accused at some point came to her home for meals, but she does not remember the date we suggest to you, not independently, rather, she has had the date suggested to her by persons who have reason to give the accused some cover for his crimes. What of witnesses V and W?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about witness Petrovic? Is not his testimony that Mr. Tadic visited him either that weekend of the conflict and stayed until dusk? Then Mr. Ljubomir Tadic testified that he came and he saw him on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He testified -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic said she saw him on the 23rd. What do you do with all of them?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Ljubo said he saw him on the 23rd. His wife said he was with him on the 23rd and the 24th. We suggest that they have, that the wife certainly has very strong motives to fabricate on his behalf. As far as Nikola Petrovic, his testimony says he was there the weekend the 23rd to the 24th. That was when Kozarac was attacked. He is not able to give you a specific day that he was there. He says, "He was at my house until dusk". The accused himself says he was at witness X's that day, the 24th, so there is some contradiction in the Defence evidence on that. We suggest that Mr. Petrovic does not have a clear recollection of which day he saw the accused at his house, 23rd or 24th. It is very possible that he saw the accused on 23rd. The accused had lunch on 23rd there and then later went to witness X's house. So, we do not believe Nikola Petrovic gives him a clear alibi for that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does Mrs. Tadic not testify that after they left witness X's house, that they spent the night, then came back, I think, the next day for lunch and then left and went home to Banja Luka, as I recall her testimony?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Witness X does live in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, this is Mrs. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Witness X does live in Banja Luka, and again what that points out is the conflict, because we have Petrovic saying, "I know it was on the weekend 23rd to 24th they were at my house for lunch. They were there for the evening"; we have witness X saying, "I remember", we are not sure how, "they came on the evening of 23rd. They stayed until the next day". She is not absolutely clear about when the next day. Then they left Mira Tadic saying, "We went home", but remember Petrovic saying, "Well, they were at my house for lunch". The accused saying that they stayed with X. So the record, as far as the Defence evidence is concerned, is very inconsistent on that point. Given the accused's ability to move freely throughout the area, and the fact that Banja Luka is, I believe, on the record some 40 or 50 kilometres away, they do not give him alibis for the night of 24th at 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. As to 26th and 27th, what about the witnesses V and W who testified here? Do they give the accused an alibi at this time? If you review their evidence carefully, you will see that, no, they do not. Witness V says that he was, indeed, in Kozarac on 26th and 27th May during the forced expulsion of the non-Serbs there or, rather, he says he was there to provide protection for the citizens of Kozarac, especially to the women and children and expectant mothers. By his testimony he did not see the killing of the policeman at the Serb church, so he cannot tell you if the accused was there or not. Assuming for a moment his testimony should be given significant weight, his statement that he did not see the accused in Kozarac that day is of no assistance to the accused. Witness V told you he was very busy. First, he told you that on 26th he really did not move from the intersection of the new road and Trnopolje/Kozarac, but he was there at that intersection. The next day he begins to move up the road. What did he tell you? The next day he was very busy shuttling people back and forth to the collection point, so that he was up and down the road. Again he does not tell you, "I was present on 26th when the Muslim policemen were killed at the Serb church". He does not tell you, "I was present on 27th when the other incident occurred". So he does not establish an alibi for the accused at all. His saying, "I did not see him" does not mean the accused was not there. There were hundreds of people, thousands of people, in the street by 27th and he was very busy collecting people. In addition to that, you will recall that witness V told you that not only did he not see the accused on 26th or 27th, but that, in fact, he never saw the accused during the period of late May until late June when he was assigned duties in Kozarac and travelled back and forth from Kozarac to Prijedor going through the Orlovci checkpoint. He told you he never saw the accused. As for Witness W, we suggest that, given all the circumstances in this case, Witness W's testimony is not to be believed. One of the things he told you when he was asked on cross-examination was that, indeed, he had watched some of this trial on TV, I believe telling you, "Nobody is going to tell me what I can do in my home" and that, in fact, he had watched certain Prosecution witnesses testify. Who, in particular, did he just happen to see testify? The man whose testimony the witness just happens to contradict, Nihad Seferovic. In addition to that, the witness is related to the accused's wife. He works for the accused's brother in Kozarac. Are those factors that automatically make him unworthy of belief? No. Are those factors to be considered when assessing his credibility? Yes. His violence towards Muslims is another factor. Jusuf Arifagic told you about the incidents where Witness W intended to throw a grenade at a Muslim's home. This was before the attacks began. He told you, "I am not afraid because I carry a grenade around with me". In fact, he was arrested when he threatened to pull the pin on a grenade in a coffee bar in Kozarac before the Serb attacks began. We suggest that when you evaluate this witness, in the light of all factors and the other testimony, his testimony is not credible. Now turning to Keraterm ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about Witness U, I think? Witness U was the Defence's, I think, first witness. He says he came down the column on whatever,the 27th would it have been? He saw Goran, shook his hand, never saw the accused.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Again that testimony of itself does nothing for the accused, because the witness did not say he saw the killing that occurred on 27th, so he cannot tell you whether the accused was there or not. Again, we are not saying that the accused was with Goran Borovnica the entire day of 27th. We are saying that an incident occurred on that day when he was with Goran Borovnica. This witness can tell you nothing of that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He says that he did not see anyone being pulled out, that the soldiers treated everyone nicely.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right. That is contradicted by the great majority of the evidence in this case. When you are reviewing the factors and considering this evidence, we would suggest that there are some additional factors to take into account with this witness. One of those factors is that the witness continues to live in an area that is intolerant, we suggest, of those who do not subscribe to the ideology of the leaders. Given that factor and this witness's presence in that area, he basically continues to live there at sufferance. Again, is that a determinative factor on credibility? No. Is that a factor you should consider? Yes.
