We suggest, considering all those types of factors, in the light of all the other evidence, that this witness's testimony does not establish an alibi for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But I guess my point was that he does say that he did not see anyone pulled out ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- as they were coming down in the column.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But I would assume, your Honour, that there were hundreds of people who saw no one called out. You remember the length of that column. You remember people talked about hundreds, thousands, of people in that column winding its way down through Kozarac and, depending upon where you were in that column when that incident occurred, you may have gone past it, you may not yet have even been there to the point that you could see the victims of 24/28 called out from the column.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He was at the head of the column, but I thought that the column ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He would have gone past by the time that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- was divided into two. I do not think I ever fully understood that, but he was at the head of the column. That is how I remember it. If it was divided into two, what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think the evidence on that was, your Honour, that it was a very long column, that as the column progressed things were happening. At some points the column was bunched up, at other points there was a separation. There was a separation at the point where the incidents on 24/28 occurred. There were people being taken out and the column basically was waiting there as that was happening. So that because it was so long there were gaps in the movement, if you will, but they were not really two columns. The front of the column would have been well beyond that point when this incident happened, the 24/28. Thank you, your Honour. Turning now to Keraterm, as for the camp itself and the evidence of the persecution in that camp, the evidence proves that the conditions in this camp were one of physical and mental horror. You will recall the camp (and we have put it on the Elmo here) was a ceramics factory. It had been turned into a camp, and that people were held basically in four major areas there, rooms or cells 1 through 4. The prisoners were there were routinely beaten, murdered, both by guards and by people from the outside. The living conditions were horrific; insufficient food, no adequate toilet facilities. People were beaten as they went to the toilet. It is in this context that the accused's presence in Keraterm must be evaluated. Witness S's sightings of the accused in Keraterm are significant. You will recall he saw him there on 26th and 27th. The accused had no legitimate purpose to be there. It was a camp set up to forcibly detain non-Serb civilians and to beat, murder and otherwise mistreat them. The accused gives no legitimate explanation for his presence there, but says he was not there. Given the fact he is there several times, the nature of the camp, the fact that on other occasions he beat prisoners there or took prisoners away from there in the direction of Kozarac and Omarska, his presence there is not mere presence but significant presence. He was connected with the operation of the camp in that he supported, encouraged, directly contributed to the abuse of prisoners by his presence there. That recurring presence is but another facet of his overall continuing involvement in the persecution of non-Serbs in opstina Prijedor. In addition to Witness S's sightings of the accused in Keraterm, three other witnesses testified to the accused's direct commission of crimes in Keraterm. All three knew the accused for some years prior to seeing him at Keraterm. The accused beat Sefik Kesic and other men from Kozarac within the first 10 days of Kesic's arrival at Keraterm. Kesic and the others were called out of room 2 and lined up outside. It was night time and the area was lit by lights from a car. The accused went down the line of men beating them, Kesic included. The accused also beat Hakija Elezovic during interrogation of Hakija at Keraterm. He beat Hakija Elezovic using his feet and hitting him in the chest. The accused used a "master's kick" such as Hakija had seen in judo and karate films. The accused also came to Keraterm and took prisoners from there in a van in the direction of Kozarac and Omarska. Witness Q on that occasion heard people from Kozarac saying, "Tadic is coming". On hearing that, he went to the door and looked out and saw the accused coming from the brick building near the weighing station. If you will look at the monitor, the weighing station, the kiosk, the brick building there he is talking about, he saw him coming from that direction towards the cells where the prisoners were kept. He saw the accused laughing and joking with the guards. Then 15 or 20 minutes later, Witness Q heard people saying, "Tadic is leaving". Witness Q again went to the door and looked out. That is when he saw the accused leaving in the van with the prisoners in it. Did the accused commit these acts to harass, cause suffering or to discriminate based on political or religious grounds? When Kesic and the others from Kozarac were called out, the accused asked each of the men their name, where they were from and if any had weapons. The witnesses in this case have testified to you that you really cannot distinguish between a Muslim, a Croat and a Serb based upon facial features. In response to many questions about, how can you distinguish? Many of them have told you name is significant. There are names that are associated with Serb names. There are Muslim names, Croat names. So names are a way to classify you into a certain group. In addition, where you are from may tell the person what your ethnic group is because there were hamlets, villages, that were predominantly Muslim, predominantly Serb. These were the types of questions that were asked of these men. When the accused beat Hakija, the interrogator of Hakija, a man by the name Radakovic, who was the director of the Kozarac National Park, was asking Hakija questions primarily about his son Salih. You recall Hakija Elezovic told you that his son had been a reserve military officer, a reserve JNA officer, during the conflict in Croatia but he was only there for a very short time, in fact, a little over a month and then he left. He came home prematurely saying, "It was not a war" and would no longer be involved in it. You will recall that Mr. Elezovic told you that during the interrogation he was told that he was to blame for his son's desertion; he had advised him to leave the military. As for the prisoners that witness Q saw the accused take away from Keraterm, the accused had no legitimate purpose for taking those prisoners other than to take them to another camp which was not a legitimate purpose. Again with these sightings and with these acts, the Defence evidence does not give him an alibi for his visits. The 27th May sighting is prior to his traffic police duties in opstina Prijedor. As for the beating of Sefik Kesic, who arrived there around 15th June, within 10 days after that, even if you do believe the schedules that were submitted to you, even if you believe they are accurate, the June schedule gives the accused multiple opportunities to be in Keraterm at night. He is listed as having several shifts during the day or ending about 9 p.m. at night. In addition, you will remember that the checkpoint is not far from Keraterm which is on the outskirts of Prijedor in the direction toward the checkpoint. The same is true of the beating of Hakija Elezovic which occurred during the time period between 9th July and about 20th July. The schedule gives the accused ample opportunities to engage in beating. Indeed, according to the schedule, the accused was not on duty on 19th July. But as for those schedules themselves, what weight should you give those schedules? In assessing that, making that determination, first, do not forget that these are schedules obtained from the force that was an integral part of the running of the camps in Prijedor, and in the persecution of the non-Serbs of that opstina. In addition, is it really reasonable to assume that if a person was a member of the traffic police and assigned to a checkpoint, he would be foreclosed from engaging in the overriding objective of the Prijedor police at the time, taking part in and facilitating the persecution of non-Serbs? What better way to give privileged people cover for their activities? Is it not the situation that such a man could leave his duties to take care of the greater duties, the persecution, and still be given credit for being on duty? Furthermore, at a time when fuel is severely rationed, when many civilians who had cars are dead, are in camps or have been expelled, is it not highly suspicious that the traffic police numbers increased over the peace time numbers? Is that not even more suspicious when you take into account what Mr. Prpos told you, and that was that the civilian traffic police were only concerned with civilian vehicles, had no authority over military vehicles or military in civilian vehicles? Yet more suspicious, in the light of the testimony of Radoslavka Lukic, who told you that there was a curfew in place for civilians from 9.00 p.m. until 6.00 a.m. In those circumstances, is it reasonable to believe that all of these people who were supposedly assigned these checkpoint duties were, in fact, restricted to those checkpoints? But what of the testimony of Mr. Prpos? He told you many things that are open to question. He said that the traffic police had to be at their post at all times. Assuming for a moment that was true, he did not say what post that would be. Of course, the post would be the post assigned, wherever, doing the duties assigned, whatever. He would have you believe that his men did not escort buses of prisoners. But Mr. Reid testified that one of the traffic policemen named Bosko Grabez, who appears on the schedule, has been named by many as engaging in crimes against prisoners while they were being taken from Omarska to Manjaca and these people identify him as a traffic policeman. A man named Zeljko Maric, another traffic policeman, has also been named as one who took part in the round up of Muslims fleeing Kozarac. Nasiha Klipic told you that he was at the separation point in Kozarusa on 27th May taking part in the separation there. Mr. Prpos's statements are not supported by the evidence. He also told you that he did not even know about movements of buses of prisoners on the roads in opstina Prijedor, though he was the head of traffic police and such movement would have impacted on his job, that is, the control of the highways in opstina Prijedor. Mr. Prpos's testimony is seriously weakened by other considerations as well. First, his denials of knowledge or participation in the takeover of Prijedor at the end of April. Those denials ring false when you consider that, prior to the attacks on non-Serbs villages, Mr. Prpos was, in fact, ensuring that weapons seized from Serbs by the police were immediately returned to them. Furthermore, immediately upon the takeover, he became the head of the traffic police. Do you think they would have given a position of leadership and authority to someone who did not have a clue about what was going on and who was not a loyal supporter of what was going on? In addition he has remained in a position of authority in the Prijedor police. Those facts make a lie of his knowledge, of his statement, that he had no knowledge of the planned takeover and his feigned ignorance of the subsequent persecution. He also testified that he had no idea that prisoners were beaten at the SUP, were brought there in buses and beaten. His officers were at the SUP and at least on one occasion when those beatings occurred Mr. Prpos was there. Fikret Kadiric told you that. Beyond the fact that the schedules were a good way to cover for other activities, another reason the schedules do not give the accused a credible alibi is that the accuracy of the schedules depends on many human factors that lead to errors. First, the testimony is that they were based on the plan that was made up in advance. The final schedule would only deviate from the plan if the people on the shift reported the change, reported it promptly, and the person filling it in entered the data accurately and in a timely fashion. The evidence shows that the schedules were in error on at least two occasions. You recall that in September, when the schedules put him performing duties in Prijedor, that police patrol warrants in Kozarac put him in Kozarac, either overlapping the time he was to be in Prijedor or having him in Kozarac at the same time he is in Prijedor beginning his duties there. The point is that these schedules are not accurate, cannot be relied upon to establish an alibi defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just to be clear on that, that is a separate schedule maintained by a different officer, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That was, I believe, the schedule about which Mr. Vujanovic testified in his testimony. It was not the traffic police schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to move to another area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. Of course, you did not mention the second mistake. Was it his position that the dates were transposed? Was it 21st instead of the 12th? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me tell you what I say to that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What I say to that is that, first of all, it shows that mistakes were made, whatever the resolution of that issue. Secondly, what I suggest to you is it is very convenient to say, as they did, "Well, when they typed up the work schedule that was posted, what they did was transpose the numbers on that". So the big schedule is accurate and that was in error. I suggest to you it is just as reasonable to conclude that, in fact, that August schedule was completed at the end of August and when they stacked all the papers up from which they were going to write that schedule, they, in fact, mixed up 21 and 12. So that 21 August work schedule that was posted is accurate, but they put that chronologically, numerically, where 12 August should have been and they put 12 August where 21 August should have been, and they were not paying attention to it. Either way, what we suggest is that it shows that these were not accurate, that mistakes were made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You indicated that the ceramics factory was outside of the city limits. Do you know how far? I do not know remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is actually on the outskirts of Prijedor itself, just as you exit the town. I believe the testimony is that the Orlovci checkpoint was approximately six kilometres from Prijedor. Since it was on the outskirts of the town, approximately Keraterm to Orlovci checkpoint, we would suggest, would be about six kilometres. So it is not that far away. It would be four to six, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can ask you this? The volume marked "proof 2", by and large, includes those extracts from the transcript which are the passages that you have been referring to? Is that statement correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, it serves a very useful purpose of relieving us from looking at the whole of the transcript and being able to concentrate on these pages.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. I would note with the exception, I would believe, in several instances where the discussion of the Defence evidence, the Defence extracts are not in there, but as to the Prosecution witnesses, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Surely, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As you were referring to S and Q a few moments ago, that was my concern. I do not know. I must admit that I have not gone through each and every of these boxes. But Q you begin with. We will locate it. Thank you. That helps.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response to an earlier question you had about the work report, Mira Tadic's testimony concerning the plebiscite, turning first to the accused's testimony at page 5913 of the record, he indicates that the voting took place in the church in that testimony. In Mira Tadic's testimony she indicates on pages 4949 and 4950 that, in fact, there was no voting in their home but all of that did occur at the church. In his work report at the bottom of page 1 and the top of page 2 where the accused discusses the plebiscite, he indicates that initially it was going to be held in his home. Then they decided to change it to the church. But in that he, in fact, indicates that there were, as you recall, "a large number of Muslims and Croats, although that particular group voted later in the evening in my home".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I recall. As I recall Mrs. Tadic's testimony, I thought that she had said that they had not voted in the home but perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: She did say that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In addition to saying that they did vote in the church area, there has been much discussion as to whether it was in the church or in the courtyard of the church. So when you say "church", it is your understanding it was in the courtyard or the office of the church?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am not sure exactly where in the church. Somewhere in that area I include. I am not saying it was definitely in the church proper.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to that, it was brought to my attention that when Mr. Brdar testified, he indicated that the distance from Keraterm and the outskirts of Prijedor to the checkpoint was three to four kilometres, to Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When we finish today, I have a number of questions about the distances, but I suppose we will wait and then shortly before we adjourn I will ask you the questions. I would really like the Defence and the Prosecution to agree, if they can, on some distances. Thank you. You may proceed, Miss Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If I could turn now to Prijedor? When we look at the evidence of persecution involving the accused's actions in Prijedor, we have two witnesses who testified about the accused's treatment of them, rather mistreatment of them, in Prijedor. Both Uzeir Besic and Sead Halvadzic testified that the accused beat them while they were being held at the Prijedor military barracks in early June 1992. Besic knew the accused since Besic was a schoolboy; Halvadzic recognised the accused in a photo lineup. In addition to that, from the first week in June until August 1992, Hamdija Kahrimanovic saw the accused in Prijedor very often, most frequently with the Chief of Police, Simo Drljaca. That evidence places the accused in Prijedor before he says he was there, if you accept Mr. Kahrimanovic's testimony to mean that beginning in the first week of June he saw the accused in Prijedor. Even if you do not accept that as a reasonable interpretation of that, it places the accused very often with the Chief of Police for opstina Prijedor. Mr. Prpos, the head of the traffic police, did not even indicate a common association with the Chief of Police. How does the accused, who would have you believe that he was a very low level traffic policeman, doing everything he could to avoid taking part in what was happening in opstina Prijedor, how does such a man come to frequently associate with the Chief of Police whose nationalism and other extreme attitudes are known to this Chamber? His frequent association with Drljaca proves the position of responsibility that the accused had and the nationalistic attitudes that he held. The evidence of his position of responsibility is further supported by the evidence that the accused was allowed to take a very nice apartment in Prijedor, the apartment of the former police chief, Talundzic. Prosecution Exhibit 367A shows you that the accused could not have received that apartment unless he had contributed substantially to the persecution efforts in the opstina. The testimony of Munevera Kulasic further supports that. According to her, while she is in the apartment and other officials are in her apartment, the accused enters the apartment and, in effect, exerts authority over the other officials, and they accept that assertion of authority. Her testimony also illustrates that the accused and his wife were willing to lie to this Chamber to make the accused appear innocent. Munevera's version of how she and her aged mother were thrown out of that apartment by the accused is directly contradictory to the accused and Mira Tadic's benign, courteous version of that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Was that the lady who, in fact, had another larger apartment to which she moved? I mean, "thrown out" is putting it rather dramatically, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Given the evidence that she presented, your Honour, I would say, no, it is not overly dramatic, because they were in the apartment. They were living there. She did not know it was the accused, but then he puts his name on the door ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- came in and basically said, "You are gone, and don't worry about finishing your food, you are gone". So I would say that is "thrown out". The witness does indicate that, indeed, they had other places to go to, that she had another apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: They were occupying a relative's apartment ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- not their own.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Talundzic's apartment. Again the import of that, we suggest to you, is the accused's ability to take that apartment, No. 1, and the fact that it was not this courteous, "Hello, how do you do? I would like to see this apartment and, by the way, I have been given it" version of events that both the accused and his wife testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is perfectly true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to turn now slightly out of order to Trnopolje and then conclude with Omarska because that then leads into the 5-11 charges. Trnopolje was a camp at which the conditions were the least severe of the three camps, but that must be put in the context of those camps themselves, because if you will look at the Elmo and recall the testimony of Azra Blazevic, it is very clear that this was not a very kind, caring collection point for non-Serbs in the area. The detainees in Trnopolje were subjected to murders, to severe beatings, rapes and horrible living conditions as well. People did sometimes come to that camp voluntarily, that is true, others did not. Those who came voluntarily did so because the campaign of terror was effective, because they had no other place to go and their only hope for survival was to leave opstina Prijedor and this camp was the main springpoint from which the Muslims that had not been killed were going to be forced out of the opstina. Regarding the accused's presence in Trnopolje, eleven Prosecution witnesses testified that they saw the accused at Trnopolje camp during the period from the end of May until the end of December 1992. Again, if you will notice, on the overhead we have prepared a demonstrative aid showing the witnesses and where they say they saw the accused. All witnesses knew the accused. On two occasions in early June, during the day, Nasiha Klipic saw the accused at the camp or going in the direction of the camp. The first sighting, she told you, was the accused in a police car, and the second occasion when he was at the tavern or the pub which was across from the camp. On both occasions the accused was in uniform. Vasif Gutic saw the accused at Trnopolje camp the day six prisoners were taken from the camp in a civilian truck. He saw the accused with what appeared to him to be a list of some sort in his hand. It was a list, a piece of paper, and there was writing on the left side, but no writing on the right side. Mr. Gutic at the time was at the window of the ambulanta in the camp looking out when he saw the accused. He saw the accused talking to the deputy camp Commander at this sighting. Mustafa Mujkanovic saw the accused at Trnopolje on two occasions, the first time on 21 August when the convoy was leaving, and that was the convoy from which later many men were take and massacred on Vlasic Mountain. He saw the accused on that date with Goran Borovnica and with others. The accused and the others followed the convoy as it left Trnopolje. He next saw the accused on 1 October when the large convoy left Trnopolje, the convoy, other witnesses have told you, was the ICRC convoy. Many other people saw the accused at Trnopolje, often more than once. Witness S saw the accused there talking to the camp Commander, Major Kuruzovic. Advija Campara saw the accused on multiple occasions at the camp between 27th September and 25th or 26th December 1992. The accused admitted to being at Trnopolje camp on five occasions. He explained those trips as follows: once with Jovo Samardzija, looking for Mr. Samardzija's sister, an end of October visit to Adil Jakupovic, once there with Ljubo to look for a friend of Ljubo's friend, the 1 October visit as security detail for the ICRC and one other visit when he says he was there to deliver Red Cross messages. Mr. Samardzija did go to Trnopolje with the accused on one occasion. He said the accused on that occasion was wearing an SMB uniform. You will recall the accused said, "No, I was not. I had such a uniform but I was not wearing it". But Mr. Samardzija, who is a retired JNA Officer, told you that on that occasion the accused had the automatic weapon and he had an SMB uniform which was the uniform of the JNA, the olive green colour uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did not Mrs. Tadic say that he was wearing a camouflage uniform and did not Ljubomir Tadic say that he was wearing no uniform? So what do we do with those three versions?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I suggest you do with those versions is that Mr. Samardzija's version is the version which, in the context of all this evidence, is the most credible. Ljubo said that he saw the accused before the accused went to the camp. It is possible that the accused put on a uniform at home before he went to the train station. The accused himself does not want to have many kinds of uniforms because he wants to distance himself from all of that, so while he must admit that he had an SMB uniform, he tells you that he had on this pullover type uniform. Certainly, Mr. Samardzija, who again as a retired JNA Officer, would be able to distinguish between the camouflage uniform and the SMB. On this occasion of this visit to the camp with Mr. Samardzija, Mr. Samardzija told you that while he, Mr. Samardzija, talked with his Muslims friends and neighbours and saw their plight, a plight which reduced him to tears, that the accused talked to the guards whom the accused apparently knew. Mr. Samardzija told you, "I did not walk about the camp because I found very early that my sister was not there, so my friends and my neighbours came to me", and the accused talked to the guards while Mr. Samardzija talked with his neighbours. That is quite a different version of the event than the one the accused told you. The accused's version, painting the accused as talking with the Muslim prisoners there, greeting them as friends and neighbours, again another lie by the accused to rewrite history, to make himself look innocent. It is totally different than Mr. Samardzija's recollection of that event. The accused's continuing presence at Trnopolje must be evaluated in the light of the purpose of that camp. The camp was a place of abuse, of rapes and murders. It was also the culminating point, if you will, for the final phase of the persecution, the forced expulsion of the non-Serbs who were not killed. This continued presence there in uniform visiting with the camp Commander, the deputy Commander, the guards, is significant presence pregnant with meaning. Even should you believe his testimony on the five visits, the accused has only given you an explanation for his presence for the five times he admits to being there. The evidence proves that the accused's repetitive presence at Trnopolje was support for and encouragement of the continuing persecution of the non-Serb population of opstina Prijedor. Now if I could turn to Omarska? As brutal as the conditions were at Keraterm and as horrific as they would be if they stood alone, Omarska was a nightmare from which far too many never awoke. The murders, beatings and abuse were continuous. Prisoners were taken out at night and many never returned. Many who did return were carried back in or had been terribly beaten. Women were taken out at night and raped. The white house was, perhaps, the horror of horrors there where the intellectuals, leaders and others were held and subjected to the most extreme continuous abuse. Men were overcrowded in rooms until they could not move, could not lie down to sleep. They were denied water during the hot summer they were held there or made to pay money or sing songs, Serb nationalist songs, in order to get the small amount of polluted water they were allowed. You have heard testimony of many witnesses who were there that during the course of their imprisonment at Omarska they lost 30 kilograms, 40 kilograms, of weight. So truly horrific conditions. You will recall again the testimony of Azra Blazevic. You see on your screens the photograph that was taken of one of the men who was brought to Trnopolje when Omarska was forced to be closed because the journalists, the international community had found out about it. You saw the emaciated men on the film, some of them so weak they could not walk without support. It is in this context that you must evaluate the accused's presence at Omarska, plus the context that on many occasions there he was not seen at the camp doing nothing but, in fact, was at the camp engaged in very brutal murders, beatings and other misconduct. Thirteen witnesses saw the accused in Omarska camp during May onward. These are sightings that are exclusive of the counts in 5 to 11 or 12 to 14 and 21 to 23. These witnesses saw the accused on multiple occasions in various places, on the pista going into the white house, coming out of the white house, near the restaurant building. Ten of those witnesses had known the accused for a long time before seeing him at Omarska. Others identified the accused through a subsequent photo lineup identification. Nine witnesses testified to seeing the accused standing on the pista. We have a diagram for you to look at talking about those sightings. They saw him standing on the pista going into the white house or the administration building. Kasim Mesic saw the accused on the pista area with what appeared to be a notebook or a book of some kind in his hand. He saw him there immediately after a man had been murdered. The accused was talking to the guard who had shot the man, with the man's body still lying there. Kasim Mesic also saw the accused upstairs in the administration building when Kasim was ordered to take a prisoner there for interrogation. The prisoner was so badly beaten he could not walk on his own and a guard forced Kasim to take the man upstairs in the administration building. As he went past the top of the stairs and past the table at the top of the stairs, he saw the accused up there sitting on a chair with his feet up on the table. Saud Hrnic saw the accused on the pista with what looked like a file folder of some type in his hand. Witness R saw the accused coming from the white house and going in the direction of the area where the dead bodies were thrown. Ferid Mujcic in the hangar saw the accused on the pista as Ferid looked down from a room on the first floor. These people saw him in daylight. Some of these people saw him from as close as seven to 10 metres away. Several facts that I have previously mentioned make these sightings at Omarska significant presence, not mere presence. All of these factors transform the accused's presence at the camp into acts of encouragement and participation in the operation of that camp, participation in the reign of terror that existed at that camp, participation in the ongoing enterprise that was the functioning of that camp. In addition, four other witnesses, Senad Muslimovic, Edin Mrkalj, Mehmedalija Huskic and Uzeir Besic were either beaten by the accused at Omarska or saw the accused beat others. About a week before the accused again beat Senad Muslimovic, during the commission of the crimes charged in 5 to 11, about five to seven days prior to that, the accused and other Serbs beat Muslimovic as he returned to the hangar after being interrogated. The accused and the other Serbs viciously beat him, made him kiss a Kokarda on someone's hat. He was able to escape from that beating, but only after he had been viciously beaten. On 16th June, the accused severely beat Edin Mrkalj at the top of the stairs in the administration building. The accused hit Mrkalj on the head with a baton, put a rifle muzzle in Mrkalj's mouth, and then raised him up with that muzzle and then began to beat him on the head with a baton while the muzzle was still in Mrkalj's mouth causing serious damage to Mrkalj's teeth and head. After he had beaten Mrkalj in this way, the accused forced Mrkalj to hit a man who was lying on the floor in the hallway. The man's skull was already crushed, but the accused made Mrkalj hit that man in the head. You will recall, as Mr. Mrkalj told you when he hit him there, the sensation and the effect was quite horrific. Something came out of the man's head when Mrkalj did that, a scream but not a scream. Mrkalj had been a policeman in Prijedor. The accused knew that. He had met him with Emir Karabasic at a police gathering a year before. At the top of the stairs at Omarska the accused asked Mrkalj, "How come you are here? What brought you here?" With a cynical smile, asked what Mrkalj's occupation was. The accused came into room A17, that was the electrical workshop room, the first day that Mehmedalija Huskic was in that room. He thought that it was probably 20th June and verbally abused the men in the room using Alija's name in a profane way. Then the accused went down the line, hitting every other man on the head with a pistol, saying to those men he hit, "You had a weapon, you had a weapon". The accused hit Mehmedalija Huskic on the head as he went down the line. The accused was within a few metres of Huskic or face to face with him during this incident. The accused also beat men lying on the pista near Uzeir Besic. Besic was sitting facing the restaurant building when he first heard yells and then saw prisoners and the accused near the restaurant building. He and others were ordered to lie down. He heard moaning and looked to see what it was and saw the accused jumping on the backs of the men who were near Besic. Then the men were ordered to go to the white house. Some of them had to be carried because of their injuries, one of the men begging to be killed. By his presence and actions in Kozarac, Keraterm, Prijedor and Omarska camps, did the accused intend to harass, cause great suffering or otherwise discriminate against his victim based on political, racial or religious grounds? The evidence says, yes, he did. The evidence is replete with references that his victims were chosen because of their perceived political or religious identity. The victims were predominantly Muslims, including Muslim police who were especially victimized, well known and successful Muslim businessmen and leaders -- another group that were particularly victimized. His actions against these victims were part of the overall campaign of terror and of taking all measures to rid the opstina of non-Serbs. The accused is guilty of these acts of persecution as well as the other crimes he committed which also form part of the overall persecution that was being carried out in opstina Prijedor during May to December 1992. At this time I would like to move on to the offences charged in counts 5 to 11.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had just a couple of more questions really on the elements relating to crimes against humanity. May I ask you them now?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The first one relates to Article 5 of our Statute. Article 5(H) says of the Rules, 5(H) says, "persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds", and both the Prosecution and the Defence in your pretrial brief have referred to that with the word "or". Is there a difference as you see it?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: There would be a difference, certainly, if you were to conclude that, in fact, what was meant was "and", then we would have to show persecution on all those grounds. It is our position that that was inartfully drawn or, perhaps, an error that was not detected and that, in fact, it means "or". We find it very hard to believe that in setting up this Tribunal they would require that the persecution on all of those grounds to be proven to constitute a crime against humanity since, in general, the crime against humanity is effected when the persecution is based on any of those grounds. So we believe that, in fact, the proper interpretation of that would be "or" but, indeed, were you to find that it is "and", we would have to prove for all three, assuming all three were factually pled and proven. The difficulty, for example, for the racial grounds in this regard is that, although we treat these people as different ethnic groups, racially you could not say I do not believe they were of a different group, although certainly the Serbs, in carrying out acts against Muslims and Croats, were separating them and isolating them as a different group. But I do not believe you would be able to say it was a racial group. So I do not believe on these facts you would be able to meet the test for "and"; yet it was these groups that were being addressed in the crimes against humanity. It was Muslims, Croats, Serbs and perhaps the other small numbers of other groups in the country. So I do not believe if you look at the purpose of the Article in the Statute, if you look at what is commonly accepted as crimes against humanity, what constitutes it, and you look at the facts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they intended "and", because I believe then, depending upon how you define "racial", it would be impossible to ever prove crimes against humanity in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose you could read persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds as being, I suppose, an enumeration of the possible grounds that may apply ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- rather than saying that you have to prove them all. It is just these are three that we consider would fit into 5(H).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, and the report of the Secretary-General concerning the Statute as well, when he at paragraph 48 talks about crimes against humanity, he there indicates that they would be committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population on national, political and here they include ethnic, racial or religious grounds. So in the report they use "or" when they are talking about those bases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: For widespread or systematic, you would have to show a multiplicity of acts, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Even given systematic, I believe you would have to show more than one act because you would have to establish the systematic nature of it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In order to prove a case for persecution, would you have to show a multiplicity of acts?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In order to satisfy the common element, I believe that you would because we cannot have an Article 5 violation unless we meet the requirements of the common element.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So if you meet the chapeau, that is, crimes against humanity, and you would have to show widespread or systematic, then could a single act constitute persecution if it was on the basis of one of these enumerated grounds?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe yes, indeed, your Honour, it could because then the issue becomes was this act done in furtherance of the persecution? So I do not believe you have to have an accused who is engaged in multiple acts as long as the one act that he or she commits is in furtherance of the persecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And satisfies, of course, the elements for crimes against humanity generally ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- which would require widespread or systematic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we were to find that this conflict was based on, motivated by, racial, well, not racial, it would be either religious or perhaps political grounds ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Or ethnic -- they use ethnic in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- or ethnic in the report, would we not then find, if we found widespread or systematic, would we not find then that every act constituted persecution?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Very possibly. If you found widespread or systematic and you found that they were in furtherance of discrimination based on one of those grounds, then it could be charged as persecution. It could all be persecution. In fact, in our indictment we have indicated that, not only the incidents I have just spoken about were persecution, but in fact all of the following counts of the indictment would also constitute part of the persecution charge.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now if I can move on to counts 5 to 11, alleging violations of Articles 2, 3 and 5 against numerous prisoners at Omarska, including Emir Karabasic, Jasmin Hrnic, Enver Alic, Fikret Harambasic and Emir Beganovic and also alleging forced sexual assaults involving H, G and Fikret Harambasic. The evidence of record proves these charges beyond reasonable doubt. On 18th June 1992 the accused went to Omarska camp with a group of Serbs dressed in camouflage uniforms. They were there to call out the non-Serb men who were policemen or well known members of the community in opstina Prijedor, in Kozarac. During the course of that day they looked for certain men and when they found them they brutally beat, tortured and killed them. There were several discrete parts of their activities that day, but those discrete parts made up one criminal transaction, the calling out, beating, torturing and killing of these selected individuals. The evidence proves beyond reasonable doubt that the accused took part in this ongoing criminal episode on that day, 18th June, in the hangar in Omarska camp. Was it the accused who committed the crimes in Omarska on that day? Eleven witnesses saw him at Omarska on that day. Ten of those people knew him before, nine of the 10 for about 10 years or more. One witness picked him from a photo lineup. That was Senad Muslimovic. Of these eleven men who saw him, nine saw him inside the hangar involved with the ongoing criminal act. Two surviving victims, Beganovic and Muslimovic, told you it was the accused who brutally beat them. Muslimovic also told you that he saw this accused cutting Jasko Hrnic like one slices chops. The accused was beating a man at a table against the wall near the water closet, the WC. Elvir Grozdanic saw him doing that. The accused was at the door to Jasko Hrnic's room when Jasko was called out. Emsud Velic and Muharem Besic saw him there. The accused was on a tyre and near one of the canals when the incident with Karabasic, Hrnic, Alic and Harambasic was going on. Halid Mujkanovic saw him there during that incident. Emir Karabasic himself told you, through Husein Hodzic, that the accused was there the day he was called out. "Dule has come, I am finished". At least one other murder victim told you, through survivors of the Omarska camp, that it was the accused who was there that day committing the crimes charged in counts 5 to 11. Through Senad Muslimovic, Jasko Hrnic told you that the accused had committed the charged crimes. You will recall Mr. Muslimovic hearing Jasko Hrnic say, "I have done nothing, Dule, cross my heart". Meho Alic, when he came back down the stairs with his son and out into the hangar, as he was forced to leave his son behind, heard "Dule, brother, how have I wronged you?" The living and the dead have proven that this accused is guilty of these counts 5 to 11. The accused and the Serbs arrived at the camp in the morning, but the beatings and tortures and murders that are the subject of counts 5 to 11 occurred in the afternoon. The lighting was good in the hangar on that day, 18th June. It was during the day and had light from windows at the outside walls and in the inner rooms upstairs as well. The hangar had been a repair facility with a big open area that used available light, so it was constructed so that there was light available. In addition to that, Witness H told you that one of the big doors was open because there was where soldiers were by that door, some inside, some outside, and that is where witness G, Mr. G, went after he had been forced to emasculate Fikret Harambasic, to spit out the tissue and other material in his mouth. The afternoon of 18th June, the accused and this group of Serbs engaged in one ongoing act of beating, torture and murder beginning with beatings of two men from room 15 and culminating five victims later in the mutilation and murder of the sixth victim of that day's crime. The accused and this group began their rampage with Emir Beganovic, a successful Muslim businessman from Prijedor. Then, when they had satisfied themselves with him, they moved on to Senad Muslimovic, a Muslim whose family was well-known throughout Bosnia and whose brother was a famous musician. After the accused and the other Serbs had brutally savaged Senad Muslimovic, leaving him in the hangar area, they called out a group of three, Emir Karabasic, a Muslim policeman, Jasko Hrnic, a well-known and popular Muslim businessman from Kozarac, and Eno Alic, a Muslim who had worked in Croatia. Fikret Harambasic was called out at an unknown time, but by the time he was forced into canal Y with H and G, Fikret Harambasic had been beaten black. The day, the 18th June, Emir Beganovic and Senad Muslimovic were held in room 15. We have provided you with diagrams, the first one showing the rooms where the people were held and the second one showing the various sightings during that day. You will see from those diagrams, as I said, that Emir Beganovic and Senad Muslimovic were held in room 15. Emir Karabasic and Eno Alic were held upstairs in this big room that comprised A15 which was the stairwell, B14 and B16, a room and corridor upstairs from the stairwell. Jasko Hrnic was held in the electrical workshop room which is A17 on the floor plan. On that day, in the morning, the accused first came upon Elvir Grozdanic, a young Muslim man who had been a reserve policeman before the start of Serb attacks in opstina Prijedor in May 1992. He came upon Grozdanic near the WC close to the entrance to the hangar building. He came upon Grozdanic, took him by the chin and asked him either if he was a reserve policeman or if he was Elvir Grozdanic, a reserve policeman. Grozdanic lied and gave a false name and locale and the accused walked off. Elvir Grozdanic told you that prior to the conflict he had an encounter with the accused when he was acting in his duty as a traffic policeman in Kozarac on a market day; that the accused and another man parked an automobile which was blocking market traffic and, when asked to move the automobile, the accused's reply to Grozdanic was that, basically, Grozdanic was a nobody who could not tell the accused what to do, and that "A day will come when you will also disappear from here". It is in that context that the accused was looking for Elvir Grozdanic or, in general, looking for reserve policemen. Later that day, the accused was seen at the corner of the restaurant building by Mehmed Alic, also known as Meho Alic, and by Husein Hodzic. He was seen by them when they went to lunch. That afternoon, the accused and other Serbs (referred to in general as the "coloured ones", those in camouflage uniforms who came to Omarska to call out prisoners and beat them) came back into ground floor of the hangar building to begin their afternoon of terror. As the accused and the other Serbs advanced from the direction of the WC, Armin Mujic, who had been sitting near the entry to the stairwell room, heard the warning that the coloured ones were coming. He immediately hurried back to return to his room and get into his room entering through A15. He was unable to get into that door because of the press of people from the outside trying to enter. As he looked back to see if he was in danger of being called out by the coloured ones, he saw the accused. The accused was with others who were also in camouflage uniforms. He says that the accused was wearing sunglasses, a hat, a camouflage uniform and some type of white belt or new belt. One would ask oneself, how could he have recognised the accused wearing what the accused was wearing? Both Mira Tadic and the accused told you in their testimony that they recognised a man by the name of Bahonjic who tried to prevent them from leaving Kozarac, although the man at the time had on a hat and sunglasses. The testimony of Mr. Mujic is that, indeed, he recognised the accused. That testimony taken alone, perhaps you would have to look at that very carefully; that testimony, however, is taken in the context of 10 other men who also saw the accused at Omarska on that date, eight other men who also saw the accused in the hangar. The accused and the seven to 10 other Serbs that he was with, having returned to the hangar, then began the beatings and torture and killings. Emir Beganovic and Senad Muslimovic were called out from room 15 that afternoon. Nihad Haskic who was in room 15 and Saud Hrnic who was in room 15 heard these men called out. At one point during the beating of Emir Beganovic, Beganovic was hung by his feet or legs by a cable and was beaten. You have seen in evidence a photo of Omarska camp showing one of the cables at the camp, that is Prosecution Exhibit 346, hanging from the ceiling in this repair facility to enable the people to carry out their repairs. After he was hung by his feet or legs by the cable and beaten, he was at some point then allowed or dropped down from that or slipped out of that, and he was told or he heard the order for someone to take him upstairs and he also heard the order "Send Senad Muslimovic". When Beganovic reached the upstairs, he passed out and was later revived. After he was revived, at some point he heard screams, he told you screams such as he had never heard before from the ground floor of the hangar. The accused and his group next turned their attention to Senad Muslimovic. The man Muslimovic later identified as the accused and the other Serbs beat Muslimovic severely as well. The accused is the same man who had savagely beat Muslimovic five to seven days earlier as Muslimovic entered the hangar after lunch. When Muslimovic came down the stairs from room 15 that day, a man in a white belt in military uniform, camouflage uniform, was waiting for him. No doubt this man was the same Dragan who had called out Emir Beganovic earlier that day. Blows from the side and the back drove Muslimovic into the circle of other Serbs including the accused. When he went into the hangar he was hit with blows from back and sides pushing him into the hangar. He was then beaten from all sides by the accused and his group. The strongest blows, actually karate kicks, came from the accused. The group was spread all around Muslimovic. They asked him where his money was, what kind of mortar he had -- those types of questions. At some point he was tied to a big dumper truck tyre. Like Beganovic, Muslimovic as well was hung by his feet or legs from a cable and beaten. The beating was accompanied by curses, swearing at his mother and by religious curses. At one point the accused held a knife to Muslimovic's throat and threatened to at least cut his ear off. Instead, the accused stabbed him twice in the shoulder. During these beatings, Muslimovic passed out several times. Once when he came to, he had been put in one of the canals, but he did not know how he had gotten there. At some point in this, Muslimovic saw a man he knew by sight, Jasko Hrnic, being dragged over. Hrnic was being beaten and cut. He heard Jasko said, or he heard the question, "Jasko, what are you doing at Benkovac?" You will remember that Armin Kenjar testified that Jasko Hrnic had been captured at Benkovac. Muslimovic heard Jasko say in response to that question, "I do not know. I have done nothing, Dule, cross my heart, I know nothing". Then Muslimovic saw the accused, the man he identified as the accused, slicing Jasko Hrnic like one slices chops. Then they poured some black liquid over Jasko. At some point Muslimovic heard "Look, he is still alive", apparently referring to Muslimovic, and he was beaten and passed out again. Then when he came to, he was told to scram and he was able to leave that area and make it back to room 15. At that point he passed out. Saud Hrnic saw both Emir Beganovic and Senad Muslimovic when they came back from those beatings. Both men were in appalling condition, Beganovic black all over his body from the beating. Comparatively, Muslimovic was not in as bad a condition as Beganovic who had been beaten perhaps even more severely, but Muslimovic himself had also been very badly beaten. Saud in that room 15 also heard when later Meho Alic was called out of the room to go find his son Enver Alic. After Beganovic and Muslimovic had been called out, and while Muslimovic was still on the ground floor of the hangar, the accused and the other Serbs turned their attention to three other victims, and that is Emir Karabasic, Jasmin or Jasko Hrnic and Enver or Eno Alic. Before Emir Karabasic and Jasko Hrnic were called out, the accused was seen by Armin Kenjar between the canals marked X and Y on the model. If you will look at the screen, Defence Exhibit 23 is the diagram where Kenjar marked for you where he saw the accused. Kenjar was close enough to be able to recognise the accused. After that sighting, Kenjar quickly went back to his room and told Jasko Hrnic that he had seen the accused. Kenjar was in A17 with Jasko Hrnic. Jasko's reaction was one of fear. Sometime following, Emir Karabasic and Jasko were called out. In the time following that, Kenjar heard screams, blows, cries, heard the command "Bite to the balls, give it a blow", like a nightmare. When Emir Karabasic was called out of room B14, he went to the window in that room and looked down on to the hangar floor and became very frightened and said, "Dule has arrived. I am finished". He then left the room. Husein Hodzic heard Emir say that. Emir had repeated previously that he was frightened that the accused would come. That was Emir's biggest worry. He would not say what had happened or why he was afraid, only that he had seen something he should not have seen, that he had been somewhere he should not have been. Emir was hesitant to talk but acknowledged to Nihad Seferovic, who was also in the room with Emir, that indeed Emir had been with a group of Muslim policemen in Kozarac when the accused had killed two of those men, Edin Besic, and the police Commander Osman. After Emir Karabasic left the room that day, that was the last time that Husein Hodzic ever saw him. During this incident the accused was also seen at a table against the wall beating someone on the floor there with a metal bar. Elvir Grozdanic saw him there when Elvir's Serb friend, a guard at the camp, took Elvir to hide in the water closet. Elvir Grozdanic told you that he saw the accused some 20 to 30 metres away, was able to see a part profile of the accused as he was beating the person near that table. This was the second time Grozdanic had seen the accused in the hangar that day. The accused was at the door to the electrical workshop room A17 when Jasko Hrnic was called out. Jasko was at his place on the table in that room when he was called out. He had been badly beaten before and had a place on the table so he could rest more comfortably. He was initially called out as "Asko". At some point the door to the room opened, the accused was at the door behind a guard. Two prisoners in that room saw the accused there. Emsud Velic was leaning against the back wall. We have on the overhead for you a diagram showing this room. In the bottom of the screen is the back wall and in the front of the screen, the top of the screen, is the front of the room. Emsud Velic, standing against the back wall, turned to face the door squarely when it opened and he saw a guard at the door and he saw the accused. Velic told you that the accused looked into the room looking the people over. Velic heard "Jasko". Jasko Hrnic did not respond to that summons. The door was closed partially. Then Jasko was called out again maybe one or two minutes later. Velic, who had slid down to a sitting position, saw Jasko make his way to the door this second time and, as Jasko was maybe one to one and a half metres from the door, the door opened, and Velic thinks he again saw the accused at the door but testified to you he was not 100 per cent certain about that second sighting. Muharem Besic also saw the accused at the door as Jasko left the room. After Jasko was taken out, Besic heard sometime later "Bite, suck. Where is your karate now?" A third man, Ferid Mujcic, also saw the accused at the door to room A17 that afternoon. Mujcic testified that he saw the accused when Emir Karabasic was called out of that room on that day, and that he also saw Jasko Hrnic called out of the room that afternoon. However, Emir did not stay in that room -- he was upstairs -- nor was in that room when he was called out. How did Ferid Mujcic make such a mistake about Emir? The reason Mujic made that mistake is that Emir and Jasko visited each other in each others' rooms. You had testimony about that. People were able to visit each other in various rooms. Emir visited Jasko in his room; Jasko visited Emir upstairs. Ferid Mujcic in room A17 would have seen Emir Karabasic visiting there. Over the passage of time, the reasonable explanation for Ferid Mujcic's sighting, linking it with Emir, was that he confused the prior visits of Emir with this occasion. As for his sighting of the accused when the door opened, that evidence, that testimony, is supported by Emsud Velic and Muharem Besic who said that, indeed, the accused was at the door, but it was not when Emir Karabasic was called out; it was when Jasko Hrnic was called out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now what do we do with that? Was that the door when Hrnic was called out but not Harambasic? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Karabasic was upstairs in another room. They saw the accused when Jasko Hrnic who was in room A17 was called out of the room. They saw him standing behind a guard at the door.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was there not a witness who saw the accused arriving, looked out the window and saw the accused outside?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Not arriving on that occasion. Ferid Mujcic after this incident was upstairs in the hangar building and looked out and saw the accused on the pista. In this instance Armin Mujcic who was inside the hangar seated next to room A 15 saw the accused in the group, apparently as they were coming back in the afternoon. He saw the accused coming in, coming past the WC, coming in the direction of the rooms A15, A17.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would that not have been after these incidents occurred?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No. That was when they were coming back in the afternoon to begin these incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But I suppose Karabasic is meant to have seen the accused out of the window?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The curious thing is that he saw him after he, Karabasic, had been called.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Which would mean that the accused was not in the hangar when Karabasic was called?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it would mean he was in the hangar because the window through which Emir Karabasic was looking was a window that looked into the hangar area. It was not a window that looked out on to the pista.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Oh?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Which room is that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was in room B14, your Honour. There are windows from that room that look into the hangar, a portion into the ground floor. There are windows ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where the canals are?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It looks down into that area. It was that window looking down into the hangar area from which Emir Karabasic saw the accused and made that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mujcic, you say that his mistakes had to do with the location of where the detainees were?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We suggest that his mistake was not in the sighting of the accused, but in saying that Emir Karabasic was in that room at that time. His mistake was a reasonable one based on the fact that Emir Karabasic came into that room to visit Jasko Hrnic. The other two witnesses support Mujcic's sighting of the accused, because they too say they saw him at the door, but they tell you it was when Jasko Hrnic was called out. Indeed Jasko Hrnic's normal place was in room A17, and he was in that room when he was called out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have photographs of that room where Karabasic is meant to have looked out of the window, have we not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, we do, your Honour. We are rustling for those now, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you like me to wait and put that on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Here we have it. That is the photograph showing that room, those windows down into the hangar area. Husein Hodzic, your Honour, in his testimony indicates he was looking down. Husein Hodzic in his testimony indicates that Emir Karabasic was looking through the windows down into the hangar area, the ground floor hangar area, when he made that remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Just prior to Jasko Hrnic being called out from his room, Elvir Grozdanic's Serb friend came to take Grozdanic from the WC back to his room. As Grozdanic exited the WC he saw two men there in the WC face down. He could not see their faces. In his direct testimony he did not tell you he recognised them because he could not see their faces. During cross-examination it was brought to light that because of their size he later thought it may have been Emir Karabasic and Fikret Harambasic whom he saw lying there in the WC. He thought that later because this was the relative size of these two men and he later heard that these two men had been called out. Emir Karabasic and Fikret Harambasic being in the WC at this time would be consistent with the evidence of what was happening here in the hangar building. We know at this time that people were being beaten until they were unconscious, that they were being moved about, and it would be certainly consistent with what was happening for these two men to have been dragged into the WC area because there was water there to revive them for the subsequent beatings and tortures that were going to be inflicted upon them. So Elvir Grozdanic telling you that from the size it could have been Emir Karabasic and Fikret Harambasic is in no way inconsistent with the evidence before you and the events as they were unfolding on the floor of the hangar. Elvir Grozdanic told you that there was blood around both men, but you will recall that Meho Alic told you when he went to fetch his son that he saw Emir Karabasic and that he was very bloody. Obviously the beatings and the abuse of Emir Karabasic had been going on. Also Witness H told you that Fikret Harambasic when he was later forced into the canal was badly beaten. That again would be consistent with the condition of these men in the WC. Grozdanic tells you that when he came out of the WC at that point he saw the accused back, as the accused walked toward part of the hangar where the big doors are away from the WC. Either Grozdanic was mistaken in this identification of the back of this man, or the accused then went around the canals and back to the electrical workshop room. We suggest to you that certainly the latter explanation is consistent with the facts. You will recall that Elvir Grozdanic wanted to run, to fly like a bird to get into that room, and his Serb friend very wisely said, "No, we must go slowly or you will get both of us killed." They were moving very slowly back to the room so as not to attract undue attention. The accused had no such restrictions on his movement. If you will see the layout of the ground floor of the hangar, it is not a great distance for the accused to have gone around the corner of that canal and made his way back to room A17.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you, Miss Hollis, point out what you would suggest would be the route that he took, looking at this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Now I know what the witnesses must have felt like! Your Honour, we have the witness coming out here from A11 and saying that as he came out of A11 he saw the accused walking in this direction toward the large doors. Then the witness goes very slowly along here moving back to his room A17. The accused of course would have no such restrictions on his ability to move quickly or at a normal pace. He comes around here and cuts through there back to the room, or he would even have had time to come all the way here and come back to the room. So either he cuts between Y and Z or he comes all the way around room Z to the room, that could be a route that he would take. The other explanation may be that unlike the other occasions that day, that the witness had seen the accused face to face or had been able to see a profile of him in the face, that the view of him from the back was a mistaken view. When Grozdanic got to the room he saw Jasko come out of the room and then slipped behind him and went back into Jasko's place in the room. You will recall Elvir Grozdanic told you that he did not see the accused at the room when he went back there. Again, we must focus on what Elvir Grozdanic's focus was at that time. The focus was I see what he described as a military policemen. You will remember that the other witnesses told you that a guard, a solider, came to the room to call Jasko out. He is focused on that man. He is not looking anywhere else. He is looking on him and a way to get back into the room. So he is not looking behind the man, looking beyond the man. He is focused on him and the door. As he goes there he is not looking to see who may be with the man in the uniform. He is focused on going back into the room. So if we have the accused standing back as Jasko comes out the door, he is standing back, the guard is standing back, then Grozdanic would not have seen him. You will recall as Grozdanic gets there it is when actually Jasko is being called out, because as Grozdanic exits he could already have been called out and be making his way to the door. You recall that it was very difficult for him getting to the door. He had to zigzag because of all the people in the room. So the fact that Elvir Grozdanic does not see the accused at the door, does not invalidate the testimony of the people who did see him there when Jasko was called out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because the accused could have moved away, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, stepped back, because Jasko is now out the door, the accused has stepped back, they are now going to take Jasko back into the other area where the beatings, the torture and, ultimately, the murder will take place. At some point Armin Mujcic saw Jasko and Emir taken toward the canal. So after these men were taken out and beaten in whatever places, at some point Armin Mujcic sees the two of them taken toward the canal. After each of these men were called out the prisoners heard cries of pain and screams. At some point in this ongoing transaction Eno Alic was called to come out. You will recall he was upstairs in that big room that you entered through the stairwell. You will also recall that the guards did not go up into that area because it was so crammed full of prisoners. So word was relayed up to them that Eno Alic was to come out. Eno Alic did not respond to that call. When he did not respond as if the horrors already occurring were not enough, the terror and pain not great enough, when Eno did not reply or come out, a Serb guard forced Eno's father to come from room 15 to find his son. Meho Alic told you how he went toward Eno's area knowing all the time what he was doing, and along the way he saw Emir Karabasic on a table near the WC. Emir was bloody. Soldiers were around him cutting him all over with a knife. When Meho paused there ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Miss Hollis, how long do you think you will need to complete your closing statement regarding five to 11? This is the last incident I think that you are getting to, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the script that I am using I have three more pages and a little explanation of the diagram that you have. So I do not believe it would be that long.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was wondering if you want to complete that this evening?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would prefer that if you would allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Continue. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not believe it will be that long, your Honour, depending on questions of course. Your Honour, as Meho Alic paused near Emir Karabasic one of the soldiers there became concerned that Meho would recognise him, so Meho was hurried on and hit in the kidney with a rifle and on the head with a knife to hurry him forward. He was forced to go on and up the stairs to his son. There, as he told you, both of them shivering Meho told Eno: "Son, they say you have to come out." Eno told his father that Eno had been told if he was called out again he would be no more. Meho Alic who had already lost one son shot on a performing stage at Benkovac, had to take another son, his Eno, downstairs to the fate that awaited him there. That was the last time he saw his son, Enver Alic, and the last words he heard Enver say were: "Father, take care of my children." As Meho moved back toward the entrance doors he heard: "Dule, how have I wronged you?" During the beginning of this incident Halid Mujkanovic had been at his usual place which was on top of lockers in stairwell room A15. He saw Emir Karabasic come down from upstairs and go out into the hangar. A man in a camouflage uniform called Emir out and cursed Emir's balija mother and hit him when Emir emerged. Mujkanovic also heard Eno Alic called and saw Eno Alic go up the stairs to get his son. After Alic went out again he heard screams and cries and men in the stairwell room began to run upstairs. Mujkanovic jump down off the locker to the corner on the right side of glass doors and crouched or knelt there on some clothes or something piled up there. We have as a demonstrative aid put on the screen for you a picture of those doors looking out into the hangar and, based on the transcript description, the approximate place where Mujkanovic was crouching by the door. As he crouched by the door there intermittently he looked out into the hangar to see what was going on. He put his hands over his face so that it would not be so obvious he was watching. So he saw portions of the following incident. He was able to see out of those glass doors the glass starting between 20 and 40 centimetres from the bottom of the door. Mujkanovic saw Jasko Hrnic's face as Jasko passed by the door, saw the guard with Jasko hit Jasko. As each of the men were called out their followed screams and cries of pain. Then two men from the staircase room G and H were called out as volunteers. There were more screams and cries. Mujkanovic saw G coming out of a canal all covered with oil. Just before he came out Mujkanovic heard noises like pigs. Then Mujkanovic saw H holding a man's hands and saw G at the man's crutch. G was ordered to bite the man's genital. When Mujkanovic looked up again there were screams and G got up with his mouth full. Then someone shot into the air. A soldier brought a live bird at that point and made someone lying on the floor there eat it. During these events the group of seven to 10 soldiers were acting as if they were at a sporting event supporting a team. During this incident as he looked intermittently, Mujkanovic saw the accused first on a dumper tyre, one of the big tyres on those vehicles, and then by one of the canals across from the WC. Both times Mujkanovic saw the accused the accused was facing in the direction of Mujkanovic. He saw the accused close to where the incident by the canal was happening. It was a bearded Serb who called out Witnesses H and G. They were taken toward a spot by the canal marked "Y" on the model and the floor plan. As they went there H saw the body of Emir Karabasic lying near the canal which is marked "Z" on the floor plan. Near canal Y Witness H saw Jasko Hrnic and Eno Alic. When ordered to pick those men up Eno Alic resisted the attempt. Eno Alic at that point was still alive. H and G were forced to drag the apparently lifeless body of Jasko Hrnic back and forth in the hangar, then to do push-ups by the body apparently for the amusement of the Serbs there, as well as the detrimental, physical and psychological impact on both H and G. At some point H and G were ordered to get into canal Y and ordered to drink oil in the canal. Then witness H heard: "Hari, come here", and another man came into the canal. Though Witness H knew Fikret Harambasic, he did not recognise the naked man who was severely beaten, bloody, black. H was then ordered to lick Fikret's buttocks and G was ordered to suck Fikret's penis. Then the three, H, G and Fikret, were ordered out of the canal and H had to first hold Fikret's hands, then hold Fikret's mouth shut as G was ordered to bite off Fikret's testicle. H was on his stomach and someone had a foot on H's neck pushing H's face into the concrete. H did not know and did not see all of the people who were in that area. He could not see what was going on behind him or around him, but heard the Serbs yelling and acting as though they were at a sporting match being entertained by this horror. G did bite off a testicle or a portion of a testicle and then spat it out into the grate at the large doors to the hangar. At that time Mujkanovic was observing this incident and Mujkanovic was telling you that he saw the accused at some point during all of this incident near this area. During his forced participation in these horrors in the hangar H kept his attention very strictly focused, and did not look around at the Serbs in the hangar. He did not see all the Serbs who were in the area. He knew the accused. He did not see the accused in the hangar area. H was ordered to drag Fikret to the table on the hangar floor and stay there with him. Fikret asked for water, but H dared not leave to get him any water.
