Then H was told to leave the area and he ran back to the staircase room and upstairs vomiting. Armin Mujcic saw both G and H come up the stairs vomiting, G all smeared with oil. This horrific criminal episode beginning with the beating of Emir Beganovic and culminating in the mutilation of Fikret Harambasic, took approximately one hour. Not long after the screams and shouts had stopped, the sounds of a truck engine starting up were heard, the small yellowish coloured truck that was used for both bringing food to the people and for taking away murdered prisoners. Some short while later Armin Kenjar heard the sound of a gunshot as though, he told you, one of them was still alive and had been finished off. About one hour later Armin Kenjar, knowing he would never see Jasko Hrnic again, wrote the date "18 June" on the wall of room A17. He also wrote the time that he was writing down the date, the time 1900 which, in his estimation, was about one hour after the incident was over. We have provided you with a diagram showing you the various sightings on that day. The diagram is, we believe, informative but it is not completely clear as you first look at it, and that is why we have provided you with copies for your own perusal in more detail at a later time. The purpose I would like to address now of this diagram is to show you during this afternoon of terror all of the different places in this hangar that the accused was seen, and all of these different places were places where the victims of this ongoing horror were being brought, were being taken, were being called out from. When you look at all of the evidence of the accused's involvement there that day, you see that the accused was an integral part of the horrific crimes that were committed that day on these victims. The evidence proves the murders. H told you that Jasko Hrnic was likely dead when he and Witness G were dragging him around the garage floor. Emir Karabasic, Jasmin Hrnic, Enver Alic and Fikret Harambasic have not been seen since that day. The descriptions of the beatings and mutilation inflicted upon them, Jasko sliced like one slices chops, Emir being cut all over his body, Fikret emasculated by a prisoner's teeth, would certainly be fatal in that place where even much less serious injuries received no medical care. Did the accused intend the result that occurred that day? This criminal episode clearly was not some random act. The accused and the others travelled to this place, had definite victims in mind, persons who were in categories subjected to even more brutal treatment than others. The acts were done to the victims in such a way as to show his intent to kill. In addition to that, the acts that were done, the natural and probable consequence of the accused's voluntary acts, was that these men would die. The intent to commit murder is proven by this evidence. The violence visited upon these victims can only be said to rise from an intent to kill, either premeditated or an intent from which it can be inferred that a person may be held liable for the reasonable and probable consequences of his voluntary acts. In this instance, the reasonable and probable consequences are the death of these victims. The accused is criminally responsible for their deaths whether he committed all the murders directly or whether he aided and abetted in the commission of some of them, or whether he took part in earlier acts and never withdrew from this ongoing transaction. His presence gave both support and encouragement to the other members of his group, reinforced the sense of helplessness and security of that group in the area at that time. With all of these Serbs around cheering, yelling, firing guns into the air, victims would be less likely to flee, to try to escape their fate even if it was only momentarily. The accused's presence, as well as the presence of other members of the group, assisted in creating an intimidating, terrorizing situation that rendered these victims completely helpless. While the evidence does not establish that the accused was the member of the group who ordered G to emasculate Fikret Harambasic, the evidence of H tells you it was not the accused, no member of that group can evade responsibility for any of the victims by claiming that he did not assault a particular victim. That is particularly true of the accused who we know was at the scene when this atrocity was being committed amidst the yells and encouragement of the Serbs watching the crime. There is no evidence of an affirmative and decisive act to remove himself from the criminal transaction. Instead the accused says: "I was not there." As for the torture or inhumane acts charged relating to this incident, the beatings and mutilation that were occasioned upon the victims that day certainly did constitute severe physical or mental pain. Several witnesses in describing the events of that day told you the cries and screams they heard were superhuman. One person said: "They were made by humans but I could not imitate it. People were screaming like wild animals." The testimony of those who survived the event proved the torture, hung by their feet or legs and beaten by the accused and others. Beganovic beaten black and in an appalling condition. Muslimovic beaten severely, stab wounds into the shoulder. The nature of the beatings and mutilations themselves is sufficient proof to constitute the required pain and suffering for torture. The evidence provides proof of more than one reason for torturing the victims. They were Muslims, either Muslim police who were especially victimized, or they were well-known and successful Muslim businessmen, part of another group who were subjected to especially brutal treatment. The pain and the suffering inflicted on them that day were part of the overall campaign of terror and of taking all measures to rid the opstina of non-Serbs. The element for any other discriminatory purpose would suffice of itself, yet here we have proof that the torture was because they were Muslims, because they were Muslim leaders who posed a threat if they were allowed to remain in the opstina, if they were allowed to remain alive, also for religious reasons. Throughout this the reference is again to "balija", the religious references. This was also done to extract information or to punish at least two of the victims. "Jasko, what are you doing at Benkovac?" That either means that he was captured there and "Why are you there?", or it means that he was being held there and that meant he could not be loyal to the Serbs. Also Muslimovic, "Where is your money? What kind of mortars did you have?" Also of Emir Karabasic, he had been somewhere he should not have been and seen something he should not have seen. As for the requirement that the accused acted at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of an official or a person acting in an official capacity, the evidence proves that as well. Look to the surrounding circumstances. The accused was in a murder camp run pursuant to Republika Srpska authority, a camp which functioned with full knowledge of and support of official Republika Srpska police, political and military officials. There were visits by officials there. The Commander there, Meakic, had been a policeman from Ormaska. When reporters went there their escorts were police, Serb officials, Simo Drljaca. You remember Mr. Vulliamy telling you that when they were in Prijedor talking about visiting Omarska, the military person there said: "Go to Manjaca, that's the better camp." Then when they persisted in going to Omarska he was told: "Well, it is not a military camp. The police are the ones who run that", and it was the police and the politicians who then talk to him about going there and it was the Police Chief who escorted him there. The acts were committed at a minimum with acquiescence of Serb officials, but the weight of the evidence shows that it was at the instigation of those officials as well. The evidence of this crime also meets the requirements of proof for inhumane treatment. The evidence proves severe impairment of these victims' physical, moral integrity or that they were subjected to disproportionate indignities or pain. The evidence proves the counts alleging infliction of grave suffering or serious injury, cruel treatment and also other inhumane acts. What of the Defence evidence here? What of Witness Z, the witness who told you he was a guard there at the approach the camp buildings? His evidence does not disprove the Prosecution evidence, does not cast reasonable doubt on it. In fact, his evidence is of no import to these charges or any other charges concerning Omarska camp, except in a way that in fact assists in the proof of those charges. What did he tell you about control over those who wished to enter the camp? He told you that, in essence, he reported for duty. That is what he knew about. He reported in for duty. Anybody in the military who is going on to a shift reports in for duty. He did not know anything about controls for other people at the entry to the camp. In fact, what he told you was: "At my post I really had no authority to stop anybody. If it was a policeman, if it was a military person, I had no authority to stop anyone. I never stopped anyone. In fact, I could not even see who was in the cars as they went by because I was a few metres below the road." So he told you nothing that would say this accused was not able to enter that camp, nothing that would tell you this accused did not enter that camp. In fact, his evidence seems to indicate that anyone who wished could enter that camp. The people who were controlled were the prisoners who could not leave that camp. What of Defence Exhibit 63C, the traffic police schedule for that day in June? That is of no assistance to this accused either, even if you give it weight as being accurate, because if you look at that schedule, according to that schedule he did not work until 9.00 p.m. on that date, well after he had committed the beatings, the torture, the murder at Omarska. But what of H's testimony saying he did not see the accused when he was called out toward the end of this criminal transaction that was taking place that day? What does that testimony mean in terms of the accused's criminal liability? First, it must be taken in context. H was not looking at all the Serbs. He was being forced to participate in their grisly activities and was not looking beyond the immediate area. Secondly, his ability to look at the immediate area was very restricted because after he was pulled out of the canal he was on his stomach, faced down with his face being pushed into the concrete, with a knife at the edge of his eye. He was unable to look around and see who else may have been there, either who may have had his foot on H's neck pushing his face down or who may have been there supporting, cheering, giving encouragement to this horrible, horrible crime that was taking place. Secondly, the evidence of the other prisoners who were able to look, who did look, put the accused in the hangar. The evidence on these counts, five to 11, prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused committed the crimes alleged. That is the only reasonable explanation for that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We will give copies to the Defence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Give copies so that the Defence will have the opportunity to point out anything that might not conform to the evidence we have received. We can talk tomorrow about the distances and some more elements I suppose as well. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10.00 a.m. 5.55 p.m. (The court adjourned until the following day).
